**Regularity convention for a possibly non-open parameter interval.** Let $U\subseteq\mathbb R^3$ be open, let $I\subseteq\mathbb R$ be an interval and let $k\in\mathbb N$. A map on $U\times I$ is **jointly $C^k$** when it is the restriction of a $C^k$ map on some open neighbourhood $N\subseteq\mathbb R^4$ of $U\times I$, in the sense of [[def-ck-euclidean-maps-and-diffeomorphisms]]; it is **jointly $C^\infty$** when it is the restriction of one smooth map on such an open neighbourhood. For open $I$ these are exactly the usual open-domain classes; at included endpoints of a nondegenerate interval, time derivatives are the corresponding relative one-sided derivatives. For empty or singleton $I$ the convention still asserts extension existence and the spatial identities below, but it does not determine time jets uniquely from the restricted values alone. The convention does not require a fixed uniform enlargement of an unbounded $I$.

**Vector witness.** Let $U\subseteq\mathbb R^3$ be open and star-shaped with centre $a\in U$ ([[def-star-shaped-open-subset-of-rn]]), let $I\subseteq\mathbb R$ be an interval, let $k\ge1$, and let $B:U\times I\to\mathbb R^3$ be jointly $C^k$ with $\operatorname{div}B(\cdot,t)=0$ on $U$ for every $t\in I$ ([[def-divergence-and-curl-of-a-c1-vector-field]]). Then

$$A(x,t):=\int_0^1s\,B\bigl(a+s(x-a),t\bigr)\times(x-a)\,ds$$

is jointly $C^k$ on $U\times I$ and

$$\operatorname{curl}A(\cdot,t)=B(\cdot,t)\qquad(t\in I),$$

the curl being taken in the spatial variables and the cross product being that of [[def-cross-product-in-r3]].

**Scalar witness.** If in addition $C:U\times I\to\mathbb R^3$ is jointly $C^k$ with $\operatorname{curl}C(\cdot,t)=0$ on $U$ for every $t\in I$, then

$$\phi(x,t):=-\int_0^1\bigl\langle C\bigl(a+s(x-a),t\bigr),\,x-a\bigr\rangle\,ds$$

is jointly $C^k$ on $U\times I$ and

$$\nabla\phi(\cdot,t)=-C(\cdot,t)\qquad(t\in I),$$

the gradient and inner product being those of [[def-directional-and-partial-derivatives]] and [[def-euclidean-inner-product]]. For jointly $C^\infty$ data both potentials are jointly $C^\infty$. No global potential on a non-star-shaped open set is claimed, and the restrictions are continuous at included endpoints by joint regularity.

Adopt as a physical postulate of this framework the following four equations for
the fields of [[def-em-fields]] and the sources of [[def-em-sources]] on the
laboratory region $U\cong I\times\Omega$ of [[def-em-lab-geometry]], with
$\mu_0>0$, $c>0$, $\varepsilon_0=(\mu_0c^2)^{-1}$ and the SI units of
[[def-em-si-conventions]].

(a) [Smooth branch] Let $E,B$ be jointly $C^1$ fields with the additional
derivatives required by each equation existing and continuous, and let
$\rho,J$ be continuous. Then, with the divergence and curl of
[[def-divergence-and-curl-of-a-c1-vector-field]] and the partial derivative
$\partial_t$ at fixed position of
[[def-directional-and-partial-derivatives]],

$$\operatorname{div}E=\rho/\varepsilon_0,\qquad \operatorname{div}B=0,\qquad \operatorname{curl}E=-\partial_tB,\qquad \operatorname{curl}B=\mu_0J+c^{-2}\partial_tE.$$

(b) [Weak branch] Let instead $E,B$ be locally integrable $\mathbb R^3$-valued
fields and $\rho,J$ locally integrable scalar and vector fields on
$I\times\Omega$, identified with their regular distributions
([[def-regular-distribution-from-a-locally-integrable-function]],
[[thm-locally-integrable-functions-embed-in-distributions]]). Let
$\operatorname{div}$, $\operatorname{curl}$ and $\partial_t$ act as
distributional derivatives, componentwise, and let $\psi$ range over
$C_c^\infty(I\times\Omega)$ ([[def-test-function-space-d-of-an-open-set]]).
Then the same four identities hold in the sense of [[def-distribution]]: the
pairings

$$\langle\operatorname{div}E-\rho/\varepsilon_0,\psi\rangle,\qquad \langle\operatorname{div}B,\psi\rangle,\qquad \langle\operatorname{curl}E+\partial_tB,\psi\rangle,\qquad \langle\operatorname{curl}B-\mu_0J-c^{-2}\partial_tE,\psi\rangle$$

all vanish for every such $\psi$, all derivatives being distributional
derivatives ([[def-distributional-derivative]]).

(c) [Scope] The postulate contains no magnetic charge: $\operatorname{div}B=0$
and no magnetic-source term appears in $\operatorname{curl}E$. Sources that
are not locally integrable functions (point or sheet sources) are covered by
neither branch and require their own definition. The equations are adopted
classical vacuum physics in the named inertial chart; they are not deduced from
charge conservation, from empirical agreement or from the special-relativity
postulates, and this item by itself asserts no covariance under changes of
inertial frame.

Let $c>0$ and let $\Omega\subseteq\mathbb R^3\times\mathbb R$ be open. A **scalar-vector potential pair** of class $C^k$ on $\Omega$, for an integer $k\ge1$, is a pair $(\varphi,A)$ with $\varphi:\Omega\to\mathbb R$ and $A:\Omega\to\mathbb R^3$ each of class $C^k$ in the sense of [[def-ck-euclidean-maps-and-diffeomorphisms]], the components of $A$ being of class $C^k$ separately; the pair is **smooth** when both members are $C^\infty$, and **continuous**, or of class $C^0$, when both members are continuous. A pair defined on a set of the form $\mathbb R^3\times[t_0,T]$ with $t_0<T$ is of class $C^k$, $k\ge1$, **in the extension sense** when there are an open interval $J\supset[t_0,T]$ and a potential pair of class $C^k$ on the open set $\mathbb R^3\times J$ whose restriction to $\mathbb R^3\times[t_0,T]$ the given pair is; the same wording is used for $C^\infty$ and for the single functions $\varphi$ and $\chi$ below.

All operators $\nabla$, $\operatorname{div}$, $\operatorname{curl}$ and $\Delta$ below act on the three spatial coordinates with $t$ fixed: for $\Omega_t:=\{x\in\mathbb R^3:(x,t)\in\Omega\}$, apply the cited three-dimensional operators to the restrictions $x\mapsto\varphi(x,t)$, $x\mapsto A(x,t)$ or $x\mapsto u(x,t)$ on the open set $\Omega_t$. In particular $\nabla\varphi=(\partial_{x_1}\varphi,\partial_{x_2}\varphi,\partial_{x_3}\varphi)$ and $\Delta u=\sum_{i=1}^3\partial_{x_i}^2u$; $\partial_t$ differentiates only the time coordinate.

For a potential pair of class $C^k$ with $k\ge1$ its **electric field** and **magnetic field** are

$$E(\varphi,A):=-\nabla\varphi-\partial_tA,\qquad B(\varphi,A):=\operatorname{curl}A,$$

where $\nabla$ is the gradient of [[def-jacobian-matrix-and-gradient]], $\partial_t$ is the partial derivative of [[def-directional-and-partial-derivatives]], and $\operatorname{div}$ and $\operatorname{curl}$ are those of [[def-divergence-and-curl-of-a-c1-vector-field]]. Both $E(\varphi,A)$ and $B(\varphi,A)$ are maps $\Omega\to\mathbb R^3$ of class $C^{k-1}$.

For $k\ge1$ the **Lorenz divergence** of the pair is the function

$$G(\varphi,A):=\operatorname{div}A+c^{-2}\partial_t\varphi,$$

also of class $C^{k-1}$, and the pair is **in Lorenz gauge** on $\Omega$ when $G(\varphi,A)=0$ throughout $\Omega$.

For $k\ge2$ and a function $\chi:\Omega\to\mathbb R$ of class $C^k$, a **gauge function**, the **gauge transform** of the pair is

$$T_{\chi}(\varphi,A):=(\varphi-\partial_t\chi,\ A+\nabla\chi),$$

again a potential pair, of class $C^{k-1}$.

Finally, for a function $u:\Omega\to\mathbb R$ of class $C^2$ put

$$Wu:=c^{-2}\partial_t^2u-\Delta u,$$

with $\Delta$ the Laplacian of [[def-laplacian-of-a-c2-function]] and $\partial_t^2$ the second partial derivative in $t$ ([[def-directional-and-partial-derivatives]]); this is the normalization $W=c^{-2}\Box_c$ of the wave operator $\Box_c=\partial_t^2-c^2\Delta$ of speed $c$ of [[def-wave-equation-cauchy-data-and-wave-speed]]. For a map $U:\Omega\to\mathbb R^m$ of class $C^2$ with components $U_1,\dots,U_m$, one writes $WU:=(WU_1,\dots,WU_m)$ componentwise.

Nothing in this definition asserts that a gauge function with prescribed auxiliary data exists, that every potential pair is gauge equivalent to a pair in Lorenz gauge, or that $Wu=g$ is solvable: those are conclusions with their own hypotheses. The signs $-\nabla\varphi-\partial_tA$ and $A+\nabla\chi$, the factor $c^{-2}$ in $G$, and the spelling *Lorenz* are part of the convention.

Let $k\in\mathbb N$, let $m,q\ge1$, let $U\subseteq\mathbb R^m$ be open, and let $f:U\to\mathbb R^q$. A map $f:U\to\mathbb R^q$ is of class $C^k$ when each component is of class $C^k$. Each scalar component uses the word-derivative convention of [[def-ck-and-multi-index-notation-in-several-variables]], whose source dimension is positive. The map is **smooth**, or $C^\infty$, when it is $C^k$ for every $k\in\mathbb N$.

Let $n\ge1$ and let $U,V\subseteq\mathbb R^n$ be open. A bijection $f:U\to V$ is a **$C^k$ diffeomorphism** when both $f$ and $f^{-1}$ are $C^k$. For $k\ge1$, a **local $C^k$ diffeomorphism at $a\in U$** is a restriction $f|_P:P\to Q$ between open neighbourhoods of $a$ and $f(a)$ that is a $C^k$ diffeomorphism. At $k=1$ this agrees with [[def-c-one-map-and-local-inverse]]: continuous first partial derivatives give the required total derivative by [[thm-continuous-partial-derivatives-imply-total-differentiability]], while continuity of the total derivative gives continuity of its matrix entries and hence of the first partial derivatives.

Let $A \subseteq \mathbb{R}$, let $c \in A$ be a limit point of $A$
([[def-limit-point-r]]), let $f, g : A \to \mathbb{R}$ be differentiable at $c$
([[def-derivative]]) and let $\alpha \in \mathbb{R}$. Then:

1. $f + g$ is differentiable at $c$ and $(f+g)'(c) = f'(c) + g'(c)$;
2. $\alpha f$ is differentiable at $c$ and $(\alpha f)'(c) = \alpha f'(c)$;
3. $fg$ is differentiable at $c$ and $(fg)'(c) = f'(c)g(c) + f(c)g'(c)$;
4. if $g(c) \ne 0$ then, writing $A_0 := \{\, x \in A : g(x) \ne 0 \,\}$, the
   point $c$ lies in $A_0$ and is a limit point of $A_0$, the quotient
   $(f/g)|_{A_0} : A_0 \to \mathbb{R}$, $x \mapsto f(x)/g(x)$, is differentiable
   at $c$ as a function on $A_0$, and
   $$\bigl((f/g)|_{A_0}\bigr)'(c) \;=\; \frac{f'(c)\,g(c) - f(c)\,g'(c)}{g(c)^{2}} .$$

Each claim asserts two things: that the derivative on the left exists, and that
it has the stated value. Both are proved.

**Why claim 4 is stated on $A_0$.** The function $f/g$ is not defined where $g$
vanishes, and $g$ may vanish at points of $A$ far from $c$; restricting to $A_0$
is forced. That the restriction still has $c$ as a limit point, so that a
derivative there means anything at all, is not free either, and it is the last
claim of [[lem-sign-preservation-near-a-limit]] applied to $g$. The hypothesis
is $g(c) \ne 0$, not "$g$ vanishes nowhere".

**Everything is proved through
[[thm-caratheodory-characterisation]].** No difference quotient is estimated and
no limit theorem beyond continuity is used, so no choice principle is spent.
The four identities are four algebraic rearrangements of an increment, each
followed by a reading of [[thm-algebra-of-continuous-functions]].

Let $n\ge1$, let $U\subseteq\mathbb R^n$ be open, let $F,G:U\to\mathbb R^n$ be $C^1$, let $f:U\to\mathbb R$ be $C^1$ and let $a,b\in\mathbb R$. Then $aF+bG$ and $fF$ are $C^1$ on $U$ and

$$\operatorname{div}(aF+bG)=a\operatorname{div}F+b\operatorname{div}G,$$

$$\operatorname{div}(fF)=\langle\nabla f,F\rangle+f\operatorname{div}F.$$

If moreover $n=3$, then

$$\operatorname{curl}(aF+bG)=a\operatorname{curl}F+b\operatorname{curl}G,\qquad \operatorname{curl}(fF)=\nabla f\times F+f\operatorname{curl}F.$$

Here $\operatorname{div}$, $\operatorname{curl}$ and the coordinate naming are those of [[def-divergence-and-curl-of-a-c1-vector-field]], $\nabla f$ is the gradient of [[def-jacobian-matrix-and-gradient]], $\langle\cdot,\cdot\rangle$ is the inner product of [[def-euclidean-inner-product]] and $\times$ is the cross product of [[def-cross-product-in-r3]].
If $f$ is $C^2$ on an open subset of $\mathbb R^m$, then $\partial_i\partial_j f=\partial_j\partial_i f$ for every pair of coordinate indices.

Let $U\subseteq\mathbb R^3$ be open and let $F:U\to\mathbb R^3$ be $C^2$. Then $\operatorname{curl}F$ is a $C^1$ field on $U$ and

$$\operatorname{div}(\operatorname{curl}F)=0\qquad\text{on }U.$$

Let $U\subseteq\mathbb R^3$ be open and let $\phi:U\to\mathbb R$ be $C^2$. Then $\nabla\phi$ is a $C^1$ field on $U$ and

$$\operatorname{curl}\nabla\phi=0\qquad\text{on }U.$$

Let $n\ge1$, let $U\subseteq\mathbb R^n$ be open and let $F=(F_0,\ldots,F_{n-1}):U\to\mathbb R^n$ be $C^1$ in the componentwise Euclidean sense of [[def-ck-euclidean-maps-and-diffeomorphisms]]. Then the **divergence** of $F$ is $\operatorname{div}F:=\sum_{i<n}\partial_iF_i$, the function $U\to\mathbb R$ whose value at $p$ is $\sum_{i<n}\partial_iF_i(p)$. The partial derivatives are those of [[def-directional-and-partial-derivatives]], and the sum is the finite sum used throughout [[def-euclidean-inner-product]]. Since each $\partial_iF_i$ is continuous on $U$, so is $\operatorname{div}F$.

Now let $n=3$ and let $F:U\to\mathbb R^3$ be $C^1$ on an open $U\subseteq\mathbb R^3$. Following [[def-cross-product-in-r3]], write the three coordinates of a point and of a vector as $x,y,z$ rather than $0,1,2$, so that $F=(F_x,F_y,F_z)$ means $F=(F_0,F_1,F_2)$ and $\partial_x,\partial_y,\partial_z$ are $\partial_0,\partial_1,\partial_2$. With that naming, the **curl** of $F$ is $\operatorname{curl}F:=(\partial_yF_z-\partial_zF_y,\ \partial_zF_x-\partial_xF_z,\ \partial_xF_y-\partial_yF_x)$, a map $U\to\mathbb R^3$ each of whose coordinates is continuous on $U$. In this naming the divergence reads $\operatorname{div}F=\partial_xF_x+\partial_yF_y+\partial_zF_z$.

Both operators are defined pointwise from the first partial derivatives of the components, so no differentiability of $F$ beyond $C^1$ is used and no orientation or metric structure enters beyond the standard coordinates of [[def-jacobian-matrix-and-gradient]]. For a $C^1$ scalar function $f$ on $U$, the gradient $\nabla f=(\partial_0f,\ldots,\partial_{n-1}f)$ is that of [[def-jacobian-matrix-and-gradient]]; in the three-coordinate naming, $\nabla f=(\partial_xf,\partial_yf,\partial_zf)$.

Let $U\subseteq\mathbb R^m$, $a\in U$, $v\in\mathbb R^m$, and $f:U\to\mathbb R^n$. If the line map $t\mapsto f(a+tv)$ is defined near $0$, its derivative at $0$ is the **directional derivative**

$$D_vf(a):=\lim_{t\to0}\frac{f(a+tv)-f(a)}{t}.$$

For a standard basis vector $e_j$ ([[lem-standard-basis-of-f-n]]), $D_{e_j}f(a)$ is the **$j$th partial derivative**, written $\partial_jf(a)$. These are ordinary vector-valued one-variable derivatives in the sense of [[def-vector-valued-derivative-and-integral]].

derivations.claim: Hypothesis check and vector step. The set $\Omega$ is open and star-shaped with centre $a$ and $I$ is an interval, and by [F2] the field $B$ is jointly $C^k$ with $\operatorname{div}B(\cdot,t)=0$ on $\Omega$ for every $t\in I$, the divergence being that of [F9]. Since $k\ge2\ge1$, the vector witness of [F1] applies and produces the field $A(x,t):=\int_0^1s\,B(a+s(x-a),t)\times(x-a)\,ds$, which is jointly $C^k$ on $\Omega\times I$ and satisfies $\operatorname{curl}A(\cdot,t)=B(\cdot,t)$ for every $t\in I$.

Converse. Let $\varphi$ and $A$ be jointly $C^\infty$ on $\Omega\times I$ and put $E:=-\nabla\varphi-\partial_tA$ and $B:=\operatorname{curl}A$. All functions are restrictions of $C^\infty$ maps on an open neighbourhood of $\Omega\times I$, so the identities below may be checked there and restricted. The field $A$ is $C^\infty$, hence $C^2$, and [F7] gives $\operatorname{div}B=\operatorname{div}\operatorname{curl}A=0$. For the curl of $E$, the linearity of the curl [F5] gives $\operatorname{curl}E=-\operatorname{curl}\nabla\varphi-\operatorname{curl}\partial_tA$; the first term vanishes by [F8] applied to the $C^2$ function $\varphi$, and for the second, the component formula of [F9] turns each coordinate of $\operatorname{curl}\partial_tA$ into a difference of mixed derivatives $\partial_t\partial_x$ and $\partial_x\partial_t$ of the $C^2$ components of $A$, which [F6] identifies, so $\operatorname{curl}\partial_tA=\partial_t\operatorname{curl}A=\partial_tB$. Hence $\operatorname{curl}E=-\partial_tB$ on $\Omega\times I$.

The auxiliary field $C:=E+\partial_tA$. The fields $E$ and $A$ are restrictions to $\Omega\times I$ of $C^k$ maps on a common open neighbourhood; the time partial derivative of each component of the $C^k$ map extending $A$ exists and is $C^{k-1}$ there by [F4] and [F9], and the class is closed under sums by [F4], so $C$ is jointly $C^{k-1}$ on $\Omega\times I$ in the restriction convention.

The auxiliary field is curl-free at every time. Fix $t\in I$. By linearity of the curl [F5] and the componentwise commutation of $\partial_t$ with the spatial partial derivatives of the jointly $C^2$ field $A$, which is [F6] applied to the component functions, $\operatorname{curl}C(\cdot,t)=\operatorname{curl}E(\cdot,t)+\partial_t(\operatorname{curl}A)(\cdot,t)$, the operators and the derivative being those of [F9]. By step 1.1, $\operatorname{curl}A(\cdot,t)=B(\cdot,t)$ as functions of the position variable, so $\partial_t(\operatorname{curl}A)(\cdot,t)=\partial_tB(\cdot,t)$; by [F2], $\operatorname{curl}E(\cdot,t)=-\partial_tB(\cdot,t)$. Substituting gives $\operatorname{curl}C(\cdot,t)=-\partial_tB(\cdot,t)+\partial_tB(\cdot,t)=0$.

Scalar step and the pair identities. By step 2.1 the field $C$ is jointly $C^{k-1}$ with $k-1\ge1$, and by step 2.2 it satisfies $\operatorname{curl}C(\cdot,t)=0$ on $\Omega$ for every $t\in I$; the scalar witness of [F1] therefore gives the jointly $C^{k-1}$ function $\varphi(x,t):=-\int_0^1\langle C(a+s(x-a),t),x-aangle\,ds$ with $
abla\varphi(\cdot,t)=-C(\cdot,t)$ for every $t\in I$. Since $C=E+\partial_tA$ by step 2.1, this reads $
abla\varphi=-E-\partial_tA$, that is $E=-
abla\varphi-\partial_tA$ on $\Omega	imes I$; together with $\operatorname{curl}A=B$ from step 1.1 this exhibits $(\varphi,A)$ as a potential pair with field pair $(E,B)$ in the sense of [F3], with $\varphi$ jointly $C^{k-1}$ and $A$ jointly $C^k$.

Smooth clause. If $E$ and $B$ are jointly $C^\infty$, the vector witness of [F1] applied to $B$ gives a jointly $C^\infty$ field $A$ with $\operatorname{curl}A=B$, the field $C=E+\partial_tA$ is jointly $C^\infty$ by the closure and differentiation rules of [F4], and the scalar witness of [F1] applied to $C$ gives a jointly $C^\infty$ scalar $\varphi$ with $\nabla\varphi=-C$; the identities of step 3.1 then hold with both potentials jointly $C^\infty$.

Conclusion and bookkeeping. Steps 1.1 through 3.1 produce, for every integer $k\ge2$, a jointly $C^{k-1}$ scalar $\varphi$ and a jointly $C^k$ vector $A$ with $B=\operatorname{curl}A$ and $E=-\nabla\varphi-\partial_tA$ on $\Omega\times I$; step 4.1 supplies the jointly $C^\infty$ choice when the data are jointly $C^\infty$; and step 1.2 proves the converse implication. The construction used star-shapedness and the joint class only through the witnesses of [F1], used the source-free equations through [F2], and used the potential vocabulary of [F3]; no global potential on a general open set, no boundary or decay condition, no uniqueness and no observability claim is made, and at included endpoints of a non-open interval all conclusions are those of the restriction convention recorded in [F1].

Let $\gamma:[a,b]\to\mathbb R^n$ be piecewise-$C^1$. If $a=b$, define both line integrals below to be $0$. If $a<b$, choose an admissible partition $a=t_0<\cdots<t_m=b$ and a continuous derivative extension $v_i$ on each piece. Let $f$ be a continuous scalar field and $F$ a continuous vector field on a set containing the trace of $\gamma$. The **scalar line integral with respect to arc length** and the **vector-field line integral** are

$$\int_\gamma f\,ds:=\sum_{i<m}\int_{t_i}^{t_{i+1}}f(\gamma(t))\lVert v_i(t)\rVert_2\,dt,$$

$$\int_\gamma F\cdot d\mathbf r:=\sum_{i<m}\int_{t_i}^{t_{i+1}}\langle F(\gamma(t)),v_i(t)\rangle\,dt,$$

where the inner product is [[def-euclidean-inner-product]]. The summands exist by [[thm-continuous-implies-integrable]]. Independence of the admissible partition is proved in [[lem-line-integrals-are-independent-of-the-piecewise-c1-partition]].

Let $O\subseteq\mathbb R^2$ be open, let $\varphi:O\to\mathbb R^3$ be $C^1$, let $\sigma=(\sigma_1,\sigma_2):[a,b]\to O$ be a piecewise-$C^1$ path, and let $F$ be a continuous vector field on a set containing $\varphi(\sigma([a,b]))$. Put $P^{*}=\langle F\circ\varphi,\varphi_u\rangle$ and $Q^{*}=\langle F\circ\varphi,\varphi_v\rangle$ where these are defined. Then $\varphi\circ\sigma$ is a piecewise-$C^1$ path in $\mathbb R^3$ and the vector line integral of the field along the image arc equals the parameter line integral of the pulled-back pair:

$$\int_{\varphi\circ\sigma}F\cdot d\mathbf r=\int_{\sigma}(P^{*},Q^{*})\cdot d\mathbf r.$$

Let $\gamma$ be a piecewise-$C^1$ path, and let $f$ be a continuous scalar field and $F$ a continuous vector field on a set containing its trace. Then

$$\int_{\gamma^-}f\,ds=\int_\gamma f\,ds,\qquad \int_{\gamma^-}F\cdot d\mathbf r=-\int_\gamma F\cdot d\mathbf r.$$

If piecewise-$C^1$ paths $\alpha,\beta:[0,1]\to\mathbb R^n$ satisfy $\alpha(1)=\beta(0)$, and $f$ and $F$ are continuous on a set containing both traces, then

$$\int_{\alpha*\beta}f\,ds=\int_\alpha f\,ds+\int_\beta f\,ds,$$
$$\int_{\alpha*\beta}F\cdot d\mathbf r=\int_\alpha F\cdot d\mathbf r+\int_\beta F\cdot d\mathbf r.$$

Let $U\subseteq\mathbb R^n$ be open, let $\phi:U\to\mathbb R$ be $C^1$, and let $\gamma:[a,b]\to U$ be piecewise-$C^1$. Then

$$\int_\gamma\nabla\phi\cdot d\mathbf r=\phi(\gamma(b))-\phi(\gamma(a)).$$

Let $U\subseteq\mathbb R^n$ be open and let $F=(F_0,\ldots,F_{n-1}):U\to\mathbb R^n$ be $C^1$. Coordinates and partial derivatives are indexed from $0$ throughout, as in [[lem-standard-basis-of-f-n]] and [[def-jacobian-matrix-and-gradient]]. It is **exact** when $F=\nabla\phi$ for some $C^2$ scalar function $\phi:U\to\mathbb R$, using the gradient of [[def-jacobian-matrix-and-gradient]]. It is **closed** when

$$\partial_jF_i=\partial_iF_j\qquad(i,j<n),$$

where the partial derivatives are those of [[def-directional-and-partial-derivatives]]. The $C^2$ requirement in exactness makes all mixed second partials of the potential available and continuous.

Let $U\subseteq\mathbb R^3$ be open and let $B:U\to\mathbb R^3$ be continuous. Given a map $A:U\to\mathbb R^3$, we say $A$ is a **vector potential** for $B$ when $A$ is $C^1$ on $U$ and $\operatorname{curl}A=B$ at every point of $U$, with the curl of [[def-divergence-and-curl-of-a-c1-vector-field]] and the class $C^1$ of [[def-ck-euclidean-maps-and-diffeomorphisms]]. A field admitting a vector potential is said to **have a vector potential** on $U$.

Let $a < b$ be reals, let $G : [a,b] \to \mathbb{R}$ be differentiable at every
point of $[a,b]$ as a function on $[a,b]$ ([[def-derivative]]; at $a$ and $b$
this is the one-sided derivative), let $f := G'$, and suppose $f$ is integrable
on $[a,b]$ ([[def-darboux-integral]]). Then

$$\int_a^b f \;=\; G(b) - G(a) .$$

**Both hypotheses are needed and neither is removable.** A function may be
differentiable everywhere with $G'$ not integrable — then the left-hand side does
not exist (an everywhere differentiable function with unbounded derivative) — and an
integrable $f$ need not be the derivative of anything
(the sign function); both witnesses are on the
companion page.

**No continuity of $f$ is assumed**, which is what makes this the working form:
the theorem evaluates $\int_a^b f$ for every integrable derivative, not only for
continuous integrands.

The functions $\sin$ and $\cos$ are differentiable on $\mathbb R$, with
$$(\sin x)'=\cos x,\qquad(\cos x)'=-\sin x.$$
Also $\sin0=0$ and $\cos0=1$.

For every real $x$,
$$\sin(-x)=-\sin x,\qquad\cos(-x)=\cos x,\qquad\sin^2x+\cos^2x=1.$$
Consequently $|\sin x|\le1$ and $|\cos x|\le1$.

For every real $x$,
$$\sin(x+\pi/2)=\cos x,\quad\cos(x+\pi/2)=-\sin x,\quad\sin(x+\pi)=-\sin x,\quad\cos(x+\pi)=-\cos x.$$
In particular,
$$\sin(\pi/2)=1,\quad\cos(\pi/2)=0,\quad\sin\pi=0,\quad\cos\pi=-1.$$

The map $t\mapsto(\cos t,\sin t)$ is a bijection from $[0,2\pi)$ onto $S^1=\{(x,y)\in\mathbb R^2:x^2+y^2=1\}$. The conventions and prerequisite facts used below are recorded in [[cor-trigonometric-parity-and-pythagorean-identity]], [[thm-sine-cosine-signs-monotonicity-and-ranges]], [[thm-sine-cosine-zero-sets-and-fundamental-period]], [[def-pi-via-first-positive-cosine-zero]].

For every real $x$,
$$\sin x=0\Longleftrightarrow x=m\pi\text{ for some }m\in\mathbb Z,\qquad \cos x=0\Longleftrightarrow x=(m+1/2)\pi\text{ for some }m\in\mathbb Z.$$
Both sine and cosine have period $2\pi$, and no smaller positive number is a common period.

Sine is strictly increasing on each interval $[-\pi/2+2m\pi,\pi/2+2m\pi]$ and strictly decreasing on each interval $[\pi/2+2m\pi,3\pi/2+2m\pi]$. Cosine is strictly decreasing on $[2m\pi,(2m+1)\pi]$ and strictly increasing on $[(2m+1)\pi,(2m+2)\pi]$. Both functions have range $[-1,1]$.

Let $k\in\mathbb N$, let $m,q\ge1$, let $U\subseteq\mathbb R^m$ be open, and let $f:U\to\mathbb R^q$. A map $f:U\to\mathbb R^q$ is of class $C^k$ when each component is of class $C^k$. Each scalar component uses the word-derivative convention of [[def-ck-and-multi-index-notation-in-several-variables]], whose source dimension is positive. The map is **smooth**, or $C^\infty$, when it is $C^k$ for every $k\in\mathbb N$.

Let $n\ge1$ and let $U,V\subseteq\mathbb R^n$ be open. A bijection $f:U\to V$ is a **$C^k$ diffeomorphism** when both $f$ and $f^{-1}$ are $C^k$. For $k\ge1$, a **local $C^k$ diffeomorphism at $a\in U$** is a restriction $f|_P:P\to Q$ between open neighbourhoods of $a$ and $f(a)$ that is a $C^k$ diffeomorphism. At $k=1$ this agrees with [[def-c-one-map-and-local-inverse]]: continuous first partial derivatives give the required total derivative by [[thm-continuous-partial-derivatives-imply-total-differentiability]], while continuity of the total derivative gives continuity of its matrix entries and hence of the first partial derivatives.

Let $A \subseteq \mathbb{R}$, let $c \in A$ be a limit point of $A$
([[def-limit-point-r]]), let $f, g : A \to \mathbb{R}$ be differentiable at $c$
([[def-derivative]]) and let $\alpha \in \mathbb{R}$. Then:

1. $f + g$ is differentiable at $c$ and $(f+g)'(c) = f'(c) + g'(c)$;
2. $\alpha f$ is differentiable at $c$ and $(\alpha f)'(c) = \alpha f'(c)$;
3. $fg$ is differentiable at $c$ and $(fg)'(c) = f'(c)g(c) + f(c)g'(c)$;
4. if $g(c) \ne 0$ then, writing $A_0 := \{\, x \in A : g(x) \ne 0 \,\}$, the
   point $c$ lies in $A_0$ and is a limit point of $A_0$, the quotient
   $(f/g)|_{A_0} : A_0 \to \mathbb{R}$, $x \mapsto f(x)/g(x)$, is differentiable
   at $c$ as a function on $A_0$, and
   $$\bigl((f/g)|_{A_0}\bigr)'(c) \;=\; \frac{f'(c)\,g(c) - f(c)\,g'(c)}{g(c)^{2}} .$$

Each claim asserts two things: that the derivative on the left exists, and that
it has the stated value. Both are proved.

**Why claim 4 is stated on $A_0$.** The function $f/g$ is not defined where $g$
vanishes, and $g$ may vanish at points of $A$ far from $c$; restricting to $A_0$
is forced. That the restriction still has $c$ as a limit point, so that a
derivative there means anything at all, is not free either, and it is the last
claim of [[lem-sign-preservation-near-a-limit]] applied to $g$. The hypothesis
is $g(c) \ne 0$, not "$g$ vanishes nowhere".

**Everything is proved through
[[thm-caratheodory-characterisation]].** No difference quotient is estimated and
no limit theorem beyond continuity is used, so no choice principle is spent.
The four identities are four algebraic rearrangements of an increment, each
followed by a reading of [[thm-algebra-of-continuous-functions]].

Let $f:U\to V\subseteq\mathbb R^n$ be totally differentiable at $a\in U$ and let $g:V\to\mathbb R^p$ be totally differentiable at $f(a)$. Then $g\circ f$ is totally differentiable at $a$ and

$$D(g\circ f)(a)=Dg(f(a))\circ Df(a).$$

For $a>0$, the function $x\mapsto a^x$ is continuous on $\mathbb R$ and
$$(a^x)'=a^x\log a.$$
For $\alpha\in\mathbb R$, the function $x\mapsto x^\alpha$ is continuous and differentiable on $(0,\infty)$, with
$$(x^\alpha)'=\alpha x^{\alpha-1}.$$

Let $n\ge1$, let $U\subseteq\mathbb R^n$ be open and let $F=(F_0,\ldots,F_{n-1}):U\to\mathbb R^n$ be $C^1$ in the componentwise Euclidean sense of [[def-ck-euclidean-maps-and-diffeomorphisms]]. Then the **divergence** of $F$ is $\operatorname{div}F:=\sum_{i<n}\partial_iF_i$, the function $U\to\mathbb R$ whose value at $p$ is $\sum_{i<n}\partial_iF_i(p)$. The partial derivatives are those of [[def-directional-and-partial-derivatives]], and the sum is the finite sum used throughout [[def-euclidean-inner-product]]. Since each $\partial_iF_i$ is continuous on $U$, so is $\operatorname{div}F$.

Now let $n=3$ and let $F:U\to\mathbb R^3$ be $C^1$ on an open $U\subseteq\mathbb R^3$. Following [[def-cross-product-in-r3]], write the three coordinates of a point and of a vector as $x,y,z$ rather than $0,1,2$, so that $F=(F_x,F_y,F_z)$ means $F=(F_0,F_1,F_2)$ and $\partial_x,\partial_y,\partial_z$ are $\partial_0,\partial_1,\partial_2$. With that naming, the **curl** of $F$ is $\operatorname{curl}F:=(\partial_yF_z-\partial_zF_y,\ \partial_zF_x-\partial_xF_z,\ \partial_xF_y-\partial_yF_x)$, a map $U\to\mathbb R^3$ each of whose coordinates is continuous on $U$. In this naming the divergence reads $\operatorname{div}F=\partial_xF_x+\partial_yF_y+\partial_zF_z$.

Both operators are defined pointwise from the first partial derivatives of the components, so no differentiability of $F$ beyond $C^1$ is used and no orientation or metric structure enters beyond the standard coordinates of [[def-jacobian-matrix-and-gradient]]. For a $C^1$ scalar function $f$ on $U$, the gradient $\nabla f=(\partial_0f,\ldots,\partial_{n-1}f)$ is that of [[def-jacobian-matrix-and-gradient]]; in the three-coordinate naming, $\nabla f=(\partial_xf,\partial_yf,\partial_zf)$.

A **compact Jordan parameter region** is a compact Jordan measurable set $D\subseteq\mathbb R^2$ that is the closure of its nonempty connected interior $D^\circ$ ([[def-riemann-integral-over-a-jordan-set]], [[def-metric-interior-closure-boundary]]). Its boundary has content zero ([[thm-jordan-boundary-criterion]]).

A regular parametrized surface patch is the image of a $C^1$ map from a compact Jordan parameter region whose parameter cross product is nonzero on the region's interior and for which no interior parameter point shares its image with a distinct point of the whole region. Seam identifications and rank failures may occur only on the boundary. Here $C^1$ is the Euclidean componentwise class of [[def-ck-euclidean-maps-and-diffeomorphisms]]. More precisely, the parametrization $\varphi$ is defined on an open neighbourhood of $D$, $\varphi_u\times\varphi_v\ne0$ on $D^\circ$, and no point of $D^\circ$ has the same image as a distinct point of $D$. The chosen pair $(D,\varphi)$ is part of the patch data.

For a regular patch $(D,\varphi)$, the parametrization induces on its interior the unit normal
$$N_\varphi=\frac{\varphi_u\times\varphi_v}{\|\varphi_u\times\varphi_v\|_2}.$$
The denominator is positive there by regularity and [[thm-surface-area-density-is-cross-product-norm]], and the vector is orthogonal to the tangent plane ([[def-tangent-plane-of-a-regular-surface-patch]]). Choosing $N_\varphi$ rather than $-N_\varphi$ is an **orientation**.

For a continuous vector field $F$, the flux in the orientation induced by $\varphi$ is $\int_D(F\circ\varphi)\cdot(\varphi_u\times\varphi_v)$. This is the scalar Riemann integral of a continuous function on $D$ ([[def-surface-area-and-scalar-surface-integral-of-a-patch]], [[def-euclidean-inner-product]]); replacing the orientation by its negative negates the integrand.

A compact **Type I region** is

$$D=\{(x,y):a\le x\le b,\ \alpha(x)\le y\le\beta(x)\},$$

where $a<b$, the continuous piecewise-$C^1$ functions $\alpha,\beta$ satisfy $\alpha\le\beta$, and $\alpha<\beta$ on $(a,b)$. A compact **Type II region** is defined analogously by continuous piecewise-$C^1$ functions $\lambda\le\rho$ on $[c,d]$:

$$D=\{(x,y):c\le y\le d,\ \lambda(y)\le x\le\rho(y)\}.$$

An **elementary Green region** admits both descriptions. By [[thm-fubini-over-a-region-between-continuous-graphs]], each Type I description is compact and Jordan measurable.

A **finite elementary Green region** is a nonempty finite union $D=D_1\cup\cdots\cup D_N$ of elementary Green regions with pairwise disjoint interiors. Pairwise intersections must be finite unions of complete shared boundary arcs and endpoints, and every positive-length internal arc must belong to exactly two pieces with opposite induced orientations. This supplied decomposition is part of the data; it is not inferred from an arbitrary closed curve.

For a Type I region of [[def-type-i-type-ii-and-elementary-green-regions]], the **positive boundary** traverses the lower graph from left to right, the right endpoint arc upward, the upper graph from right to left, and the left endpoint arc downward, omitting zero-length arcs. For a Type II description it traverses the right graph upward, the top endpoint arc from right to left, the left graph downward, and the bottom endpoint arc from left to right. In both cases the region remains locally on the left.

For a finite elementary Green region, delete every shared internal arc together with its oppositely oriented copy and retain the orientations of all surviving arcs. Reversal and concatenation are those of [[def-piecewise-c1-path-operations-and-oriented-reparametrizations]].

The surviving arcs form a finite list $\sigma_1,\ldots,\sigma_m$ of oriented piecewise-$C^1$ arcs, called the **positive boundary chain** $\partial D$. A finite elementary Green region need not be connected and need not be simply connected, so this list need not assemble into a single closed path. Accordingly, for a continuous field $G$ on a neighbourhood of $D$ the boundary integral is defined as the finite sum

$$\int_{\partial D}G\cdot d\mathbf r:=\sum_{k=1}^m\int_{\sigma_k}G\cdot d\mathbf r,$$

and likewise $\int_{\partial D}P\,dx+Q\,dy$ for the field $(P,Q)$. When the surviving arcs do assemble into one closed path — in particular for a single elementary region, whose positive boundary is the concatenation of its four arcs — this sum is that path's integral, because vector line integrals add under concatenation ([[thm-line-integrals-under-reversal-and-concatenation]]). The value is independent of the order of the list, since a finite sum of reals does not depend on its order.

A **$C^2$ patch over a finite elementary Green region** is a regular parametrized surface patch $(D,\varphi)$ in the sense of [[def-admissible-regular-parametrized-surface-patch]] whose parameter region $D$ is supplied, in addition, with a decomposition making it a finite elementary Green region in the sense of [[def-type-i-type-ii-and-elementary-green-regions]], and whose parametrization $\varphi$ is of class $C^2$ on an open neighbourhood of $D$ ([[def-ck-euclidean-maps-and-diffeomorphisms]]). Both requirements on $D$ are part of the data: it is a compact Jordan parameter region, so it is the closure of its nonempty connected interior, and it carries a supplied elementary decomposition.

Let $\partial D=(\sigma_1,\ldots,\sigma_m)$ be the positive boundary chain of that decomposition, the finite list of oriented piecewise-$C^1$ arcs of [[def-positive-orientation-for-elementary-region-boundaries]]. Then the **induced boundary chain** is the list of arcs obtained by composing the positive boundary chain of the parameter region with the parametrization, namely

$$\varphi(\partial D):=(\varphi\circ\sigma_1,\ldots,\varphi\circ\sigma_m),$$

each entry a piecewise-$C^1$ path in $\mathbb R^3$ in the sense of [[def-piecewise-c1-path-operations-and-oriented-reparametrizations]]. For a continuous vector field $F$ on a set containing $\varphi[D]$, the **circulation of $F$ around the induced boundary chain** is the finite sum

$$\oint_{\varphi(\partial D)}F\cdot d\mathbf r:=\sum_{l=1}^m\int_{\varphi\circ\sigma_l}F\cdot d\mathbf r,$$

with the vector line integrals of [[def-scalar-and-vector-line-integrals-along-piecewise-c1-paths]]. The value does not depend on the order of the list, a finite sum of reals being independent of its order.

If instead $F$ is defined on an open set $U$ containing $\varphi[D]$, continuity of $\varphi$ and compactness of $D$ give an open neighbourhood $V$ of $D$ in the domain of $\varphi$ with $\varphi[V]\subseteq U$. On $V$, the **pulled-back functions** are the inner products of the field along the parametrization with the two parameter derivatives:

$$P^{*}:=\langle F\circ\varphi,\varphi_u\rangle,\qquad Q^{*}:=\langle F\circ\varphi,\varphi_v\rangle,$$

with the inner product of [[def-euclidean-inner-product]]. The oriented area vector $\varphi_u\times\varphi_v$ and the flux it computes are those of [[def-oriented-unit-normal-and-flux-of-a-surface-patch]]. A merely continuous field on an arbitrary set containing $\varphi[D]$ is enough for circulation, but not for these neighbourhood-defined pullbacks.

Let $(D,\varphi)$ be a $C^2$ patch over a finite elementary Green region ([[def-the-induced-boundary-chain-of-a-c2-surface-patch]]), with positive boundary chain $\partial D=(\sigma_1,\ldots,\sigma_m)$ and induced boundary chain $\varphi(\partial D)$, and let $F$ be a $C^1$ vector field on an open set $U\subseteq\mathbb R^3$ containing $\varphi[D]$. Then the circulation around the induced boundary chain equals the flux of the curl in the induced orientation:

$$\oint_{\varphi(\partial D)}F\cdot d\mathbf r=\int_D\bigl\langle(\operatorname{curl}F)\circ\varphi,\ \varphi_u\times\varphi_v\bigr\rangle.$$

The right-hand side is the flux of $\operatorname{curl}F$ through the patch in the orientation induced by $\varphi$, in the sense of [[def-oriented-unit-normal-and-flux-of-a-surface-patch]].

Let $n \in \mathbb{N}$. A natural number is a von Neumann natural, that is a set,
and $n = \{0, 1, \dots, n-1\}$ ([[def-natural-numbers]],
[[lem-nat-order-is-membership]]), so

$$\mathbb{R}^{n} \;=\; \{\, x \;:\; x \text{ is a function } n \to \mathbb{R} \,\}$$

is the function space of [[def-function-space]] at $F = \mathbb{R}$ and $X = n$,
a vector space over $\mathbb{R}$ under the pointwise operations
([[def-vector-space]]). We write $x_k := x(k)$ for $k < n$, and two elements of
$\mathbb{R}^{n}$ are equal exactly when they agree at every $k < n$. This is the
same set that [[lem-metrics-on-rn]] calls $\mathbb{R}^{n}$.

The **Euclidean inner product** of $x, y \in \mathbb{R}^{n}$ is the real number

$$\langle x, y\rangle \;:=\; \sum_{k<n} x_k\,y_k ,$$

the finite sum of [[def-finite-sum]] applied to the list $k \mapsto x_k y_k$
(extended by $0$ beyond $n$, as every finite list in this library is). The
**Euclidean norm** of $x$ is

$$\lVert x\rVert_2 \;:=\; \sqrt{\langle x, x\rangle},$$

which is defined because $\langle x,x\rangle = \sum_{k<n} x_k^{2} \ge 0$ (a sum
of nonnegative terms, [[lem-finite-sum-laws]] clause 4 and
[[lem-of-square-positive]], the case $x_k = 0$ giving $x_k^2 = 0$ by
[[def-integer-power]]) and every nonnegative real has a unique nonnegative square
root ([[thm-of-square-roots]]).

### Both are defined for every $n$, including $n = 0$

At $n = 0$ the set $\mathbb{R}^{0}$ has exactly one element, the empty function,
and it is the zero vector space ([[lem-standard-basis-of-f-n]] clause 5); the sum
above is the empty sum, so $\langle x,y\rangle = 0$ and $\lVert x\rVert_2 = 0$.
**This is the first place on this page where the two index regimes diverge, and
the divergence is deliberate.** The published metrics $d_1$, $d_2$, $d_\infty$ of
[[lem-metrics-on-rn]] are defined only for $n \ge 1$, because $d_\infty$ would
otherwise be a maximum over the empty index set; the algebra above needs no such
restriction. The boundary in this page runs between the algebra and the metric,
not where a reader would guess, and [[rem-rn-conventions-and-scope]] lists
exactly which items inherit $n \ge 1$.

### The algebra of the inner product

For all $x, y, z \in \mathbb{R}^{n}$ and $\lambda \in \mathbb{R}$:

1. **Symmetry.** $\langle x,y\rangle = \langle y,x\rangle$, since $x_ky_k = y_kx_k$
   termwise.
2. **Additivity in the first argument.**
   $\langle x + y, z\rangle = \langle x,z\rangle + \langle y,z\rangle$: the list
   $k \mapsto (x_k+y_k)z_k$ is the termwise sum of $k \mapsto x_kz_k$ and
   $k \mapsto y_kz_k$, so [[lem-finite-sum-laws]] clause 1 applies.
3. **Homogeneity in the first argument.**
   $\langle \lambda x, y\rangle = \lambda\langle x,y\rangle$, by
   [[lem-finite-sum-laws]] clause 2.
4. **Bilinearity.** Clauses 2 and 3 together with symmetry give the same two laws
   in the second argument.
5. **Positive definiteness.** $\langle x,x\rangle \ge 0$, and
   $\langle x,x\rangle = 0$ if and only if $x = 0$. Indeed a vanishing sum of
   nonnegative terms has every term $0$ ([[lem-finite-sum-laws]] clause 4), so
   $x_k^{2} = 0$ for every $k < n$, and a nonzero real has a positive square
   ([[lem-of-square-positive]]), whence $x_k = 0$ for every $k < n$ and $x = 0$.
6. **Agreement with the published Euclidean metric.** For $n \ge 1$ and
   $x, y \in \mathbb{R}^{n}$,
   $\lVert x - y\rVert_2 = \sqrt{\sum_{k<n}(x_k-y_k)^{2}} = d_2(x,y)$, the two
   sides being the same expression ([[lem-metrics-on-rn]]). In particular
   $\lVert x\rVert_2 = d_2(x, 0)$.

That $\lVert\cdot\rVert_2$ is a norm in the sense of [[def-norm-and-normed-space]]
is proved in [[thm-cauchy-schwarz-and-the-euclidean-norm]], where the triangle
inequality is obtained from the Cauchy-Schwarz inequality; it is not assumed
here.

For $u=(u_x,u_y,u_z)$ and $v=(v_x,v_y,v_z)$ in $\mathbb R^3$, define $u\times v=(u_yv_z-u_zv_y,\,u_zv_x-u_xv_z,\,u_xv_y-u_yv_x)$.

This is the right-handed **cross product**. The displayed coordinates are those of the standard basis ([[lem-standard-basis-of-f-n]]), and inner products and norms are those of [[def-euclidean-inner-product]].
For all $u,v,w\in\mathbb R^3$, the cross product is bilinear and alternating, $\langle u\times v,w\rangle=\det[u\ v\ w]$, and $u\times v$ is orthogonal to both $u$ and $v$.

Let $E\subseteq\mathbb R^m$ be bounded in the metric sense of
[[def-metric-bounded-diameter]] and Jordan measurable, and let
$f:E\to\mathbb R$ be bounded. Choose a nondegenerate rectangle
$Q\supseteq E$, whose existence follows from
[[def-jordan-inner-and-outer-content]], and define the zero extension
$$\widetilde f_Q(x):=\begin{cases}f(x),&x\in E,\\0,&x\in Q\setminus E.\end{cases}$$
The function $f$ is **Riemann integrable over $E$** when $\widetilde f_Q$ is integrable over $Q$, and then
$$\int_Ef:=\int_Q\widetilde f_Q.$$
Independence of the bounding rectangle, for both integrability and value, is proved in [[lem-jordan-set-integral-well-defined]] and recorded as the definition's forward justification. For $f=1$, the zero extension is $1_E$, so [[thm-jordan-content-and-indicator-integrability]] gives $\int_E1=\operatorname{cont}(E)$.

Let $E\subseteq\mathbb R^{p+q}$ be a bounded Jordan set and let $g:E\to\mathbb R$ be Riemann integrable. Suppose that for all $x$ outside a content-zero set $N\subseteq\mathbb R^p$, the section $E_x$ is Jordan measurable and $g_x$ is integrable over it. Put $h(x)=\int_{E_x}g_x$ there and assign arbitrary bounded values to $h$ on $N$, with empty-section integral equal to $0$. Then $h$ is integrable on any rectangle containing the projection of $E$, its integral is independent of that rectangle and of the values on $N$, and
$$\int_Eg=\int h(x)\,dx.$$
The symmetric assertion holds for the other coordinate block.

Throughout, $I := [0,1] = \{\, t \in \mathbb{R} : 0 \le t \le 1 \,\}$
([[def-interval]]) carries the subspace topology inherited from $\mathbb{R}$ with
its usual topology ([[def-subspace-topology-top]],
[[lem-real-line-is-a-metric-space]], [[def-metric-topology]],
[[def-metrizable-space]]). It is called the **unit interval**.

Let $X$ be a topological space ([[def-topological-space]]) and let
$x, y \in X$.

- A **path in $X$ from $x$ to $y$** is a continuous map $\gamma : I \to X$
  ([[def-continuous-map-top]]) with $\gamma(0) = x$ and $\gamma(1) = y$. Its
  **image** is $\gamma[I]$.
- $X$ is **path-connected** when for every pair $x, y \in X$ there is a path in
  $X$ from $x$ to $y$. A subset $A \subseteq X$ is a **path-connected subset**
  when the space $A$ with its subspace topology is path-connected; equivalently,
  when any two of its points are joined by a path whose image lies in $A$, by the
  characteristic property of a map into a subspace
  ([[def-subspace-topology-top]]).
- Write $x \sim y$ when a path in $X$ from $x$ to $y$ exists. The **path
  component** of $x$ is its equivalence class
  $$P(x) \;:=\; \{\, y \in X : x \sim y \,\} .$$
- The empty space is path-connected, the defining condition quantifying over no
  pair of points, and so is every one-point space, the constant path joining its
  point to itself.

**$\sim$ is an equivalence relation on $X$, and the obligation is discharged
here**, so that "equivalence class" above denotes.

*Reflexive.* The constant map $\gamma(t) = x$ is continuous, every preimage being
$\varnothing$ or $I$ ([[def-continuous-map-top]]), and joins $x$ to $x$.

*Symmetric.* If $\gamma$ joins $x$ to $y$, put $\bar\gamma(t) := \gamma(1-t)$.
The map $r : I \to I$, $r(t) = 1 - t$, is continuous: for $s, t \in I$ one has
$|r(s) - r(t)| = |s - t|$, so a ball of radius $\varepsilon$ around $r(t)$ pulls
back to contain the ball of radius $\varepsilon$ around $t$
([[def-metric-ball]], [[def-metrizable-space]]). Hence
$\bar\gamma = \gamma \circ r$ is continuous ([[lem-continuity-is-local-and-pastes]],
claim 1) and joins $y$ to $x$.

*Transitive.* Let $\gamma_1$ join $x$ to $y$ and $\gamma_2$ join $y$ to $z$.
Define $\delta : I \to X$ by

$$\delta(t) \;:=\; \begin{cases} \gamma_1(2t), & 0 \le t \le 1/2, \\ \gamma_2(2t - 1), & 1/2 \le t \le 1. \end{cases}$$

The two clauses agree at $t = 1/2$, both giving $\gamma_1(1) = y = \gamma_2(0)$,
so $\delta$ is a well-defined function. The sets $[0,1/2]$ and $[1/2,1]$ are
closed in $I$ and cover it, and there are **two** of them, so the finite closed
form of the pasting lemma applies ([[lem-continuity-is-local-and-pastes]],
claim 3). On $[0,1/2]$ the map $\delta$ is $\gamma_1 \circ a_1$ with
$a_1(t) = 2t$, and on $[1/2,1]$ it is $\gamma_2 \circ a_2$ with
$a_2(t) = 2t - 1$; each $a_k$ is continuous into $I$, since
$|a_k(s) - a_k(t)| = 2|s-t|$, so the ball of radius $\varepsilon/2$ around $t$
maps into the ball of radius $\varepsilon$ around $a_k(t)$
([[def-metric-ball]], [[def-metrizable-space]],
[[def-subspace-topology-top]]). So both restrictions are continuous by
[[lem-continuity-is-local-and-pastes]] claim 1, hence $\delta$ is continuous, and
it joins $x$ to $z$.

**The path components partition $X$**, being the classes of an equivalence
relation, and each is a path-connected subset of $X$: two points of $P(x)$ are
joined to $x$, hence to each other by the transitivity construction above, and
the resulting path has image inside $P(x)$: if $\delta$ is a path from $x$ and
$s \in I$, then $t \mapsto \delta(st)$ is a path from $x$ to $\delta(s)$,
continuous because $t \mapsto st$ satisfies $|st_1 - st_2| \le |t_1 - t_2|$ and
is therefore continuous into $I$ by the ball criterion used above, so every point
of the image is itself joined to $x$.

Let $X$ be a topological space and let $x_0\in X$. A **based loop at $x_0$**
is a path $\alpha:I\to X$ with $\alpha(0)=x_0=\alpha(1)$
([[def-path-connected]]). Two based loops are equivalent when they are
path-homotopic relative to the endpoints. This is an equivalence relation by
[[cor-homotopy-relative-and-path-homotopy-are-equivalence-relations]].

The **fundamental group set** of $X$ at $x_0$ is

$$\pi_1(X,x_0):=\{\,[\alpha]:\alpha\text{ is a based loop at }x_0\,\}.$$

For composable paths, write

$$(\alpha*\beta)(s):=\begin{cases}\alpha(2s),&0\leq s\leq\tfrac12,\\ \beta(2s-1),&\tfrac12\leq s\leq1.\end{cases}$$

The finite closed-pasting argument already carried out in
[[def-path-connected]] shows that this is a path. The multiplication proposed
on loop classes is

$$[\alpha][\beta]:=[\alpha*\beta].$$

**Order convention.** The product $[\alpha][\beta]$ traverses $\alpha$ first
and $\beta$ second. Every product on this page uses this convention.

The constant loop at $x_0$ is denoted $c_{x_0}$, and the reversed loop is
$\bar\alpha(s):=\alpha(1-s)$. The next theorem proves that multiplication is
independent of representatives and that $[c_{x_0}]$ and $[\bar\alpha]$ are the
identity and inverse required by the group axioms.

Write $I=[0,1]$ with its usual subspace topology, as in [[def-path-connected]]. Let $X$ and $Y$ be topological spaces, and let $f,g:X\to Y$ be continuous maps ([[def-continuous-map-top]]).

A **homotopy from $f$ to $g$** is a continuous map

$$H:X\times I\longrightarrow Y$$

from the product space ([[def-product-topology]]) such that $H(x,0)=f(x)$ and $H(x,1)=g(x)$ for every $x\in X$. When such an $H$ exists, $f$ and $g$ are **homotopic**, written $f\simeq g$.

Let $A\subseteq X$ carry the subspace topology ([[def-subspace-topology-top]]). The homotopy $H$ is a **homotopy relative to $A$**, or a homotopy **rel $A$**, when

$$H(a,t)=f(a)=g(a)\qquad(a\in A,\ t\in I).$$

Thus a homotopy rel $A$ can exist only when $f|_A=g|_A$, and every ordinary homotopy is a homotopy rel $\varnothing$. We write $f\simeq_A g$ when a homotopy rel $A$ exists.

If $\alpha,\beta:I\to Y$ are paths with the same initial point and the same terminal point ([[def-path-connected]]), a **path homotopy from $\alpha$ to $\beta$ relative to the endpoints** is a homotopy $H:I\times I\to Y$ rel $\{0,1\}$. Explicitly,

$$H(s,0)=\alpha(s),\quad H(s,1)=\beta(s),\quad H(0,t)=\alpha(0)=\beta(0),\quad H(1,t)=\alpha(1)=\beta(1).$$

The first coordinate $s$ parametrises the path and the second coordinate $t$ parametrises the deformation.

For fixed spaces $X,Y$ and a fixed subspace $A\subseteq X$, the relation $\simeq_A$ is an equivalence relation on the set of continuous maps $X\to Y$ that have a prescribed restriction to $A$. In particular ordinary homotopy is an equivalence relation on the continuous maps $X\to Y$.

For fixed endpoints $y_0,y_1\in Y$, path homotopy relative to the endpoints is an equivalence relation on the set of paths from $y_0$ to $y_1$.

For $n\ge1$, put $P=\mathbb R^n\setminus\{0\}$ and define

$$H:P\times[0,1]\to P,\qquad H(x,t)=\bigl((1-t)+t/\lVert x\rVert_2\bigr)x.$$

Then $H$ is continuous, $H(x,0)=x$, $H(x,1)=x/\lVert x\rVert_2$, $H(s,t)=s$ for $s\in S^{n-1}$, and $H(x,t)\ne0$.
For $n\ge1$, the map $\rho:\mathbb R^n\setminus\{0\}\to S^{n-1}$ defined by $\rho(x)=x/\lVert x\rVert_2$ is continuous.

A topological space $X$ is **simply connected** when it is nonempty and
path-connected ([[def-path-connected]]) and, for every $x_0\in X$, the group
$\pi_1(X,x_0)$ has exactly one element.

Requiring every basepoint avoids presuming a change-of-basepoint theorem. For a
path-connected space that later theorem shows that checking one basepoint is
equivalent, but no such result is needed for this definition. The empty space
is path-connected under the published convention, but it is not simply
connected here because nonemptiness is explicit.
For every natural number $n\ge2$, the unit sphere $S^n\subseteq\mathbb R^{n+1}$ is simply connected ([[def-simply-connected]]).
For $n\ge2$, the unit sphere $S^{n-1}\subseteq\mathbb R^n$ is path-connected and connected.

Let $X$ be a topological space, with subsets carrying the subspace topology
([[def-subspace-topology-top]]). Then:

1. **The unit interval is connected.** $I = [0,1]$ is a connected subset of
   $\mathbb{R}$, hence a connected space.
2. **Path-connected implies connected.** If $X$ is path-connected
   ([[def-path-connected]]) then $X$ is connected ([[def-connected-space]]). The
   same holds for a subset: a path-connected subset of $X$ is a connected subset
   of $X$.
3. **Path components refine components.** For every $x \in X$,
   $$P(x) \;\subseteq\; C(x),$$
   the path component inside the component
   ([[def-connected-component-and-quasicomponent]]). So every component is a
   union of path components.

**No converse is claimed.** Claim 2 is one-directional and claim 3 is an
inclusion; the question of when a connected space is path-connected is not
settled here.

**No choice principle is used.** The proof takes the union over the **set of all**
paths issuing from a fixed point rather than selecting one path per endpoint,
which is what an appeal to the Axiom of Choice would be. The point at which the
temptation arises is flagged in the remarks.

Let $X$ and $Y$ be normed spaces over the same scalar field, and assume $X$
admits an ordered basis of finite length. Then every linear map $S:X\to Y$ is a
bounded linear operator in the sense of [[def-bounded-linear-operator]].

Let $X$ and $Y$ be normed spaces over the same scalar field, and let
$T:X\to Y$ be linear. Then the following are equivalent:

1. $T$ is bounded.
2. $T$ is continuous at $0$.
3. $T$ is continuous on $X$.
4. $T$ is Lipschitz.

Let $f,g:X\to\mathbb R$ be continuous maps from a topological space. Then
$f+g$, $fg$, $|f|$, $\max(f,g)$, and $\min(f,g)$ are continuous. On the open
cozero set $\operatorname{coz}(g)$, the quotient $f/g$ is continuous. The same
holds for every finite sum, product, maximum, or minimum of continuous
real-valued maps.

Adopt as a physical postulate of this framework the following four equations for
the fields of [[def-em-fields]] and the sources of [[def-em-sources]] on the
laboratory region $U\cong I\times\Omega$ of [[def-em-lab-geometry]], with
$\mu_0>0$, $c>0$, $\varepsilon_0=(\mu_0c^2)^{-1}$ and the SI units of
[[def-em-si-conventions]].

(a) [Smooth branch] Let $E,B$ be jointly $C^1$ fields with the additional
derivatives required by each equation existing and continuous, and let
$\rho,J$ be continuous. Then, with the divergence and curl of
[[def-divergence-and-curl-of-a-c1-vector-field]] and the partial derivative
$\partial_t$ at fixed position of
[[def-directional-and-partial-derivatives]],

$$\operatorname{div}E=\rho/\varepsilon_0,\qquad \operatorname{div}B=0,\qquad \operatorname{curl}E=-\partial_tB,\qquad \operatorname{curl}B=\mu_0J+c^{-2}\partial_tE.$$

(b) [Weak branch] Let instead $E,B$ be locally integrable $\mathbb R^3$-valued
fields and $\rho,J$ locally integrable scalar and vector fields on
$I\times\Omega$, identified with their regular distributions
([[def-regular-distribution-from-a-locally-integrable-function]],
[[thm-locally-integrable-functions-embed-in-distributions]]). Let
$\operatorname{div}$, $\operatorname{curl}$ and $\partial_t$ act as
distributional derivatives, componentwise, and let $\psi$ range over
$C_c^\infty(I\times\Omega)$ ([[def-test-function-space-d-of-an-open-set]]).
Then the same four identities hold in the sense of [[def-distribution]]: the
pairings

$$\langle\operatorname{div}E-\rho/\varepsilon_0,\psi\rangle,\qquad \langle\operatorname{div}B,\psi\rangle,\qquad \langle\operatorname{curl}E+\partial_tB,\psi\rangle,\qquad \langle\operatorname{curl}B-\mu_0J-c^{-2}\partial_tE,\psi\rangle$$

all vanish for every such $\psi$, all derivatives being distributional
derivatives ([[def-distributional-derivative]]).

(c) [Scope] The postulate contains no magnetic charge: $\operatorname{div}B=0$
and no magnetic-source term appears in $\operatorname{curl}E$. Sources that
are not locally integrable functions (point or sheet sources) are covered by
neither branch and require their own definition. The equations are adopted
classical vacuum physics in the named inertial chart; they are not deduced from
charge conservation, from empirical agreement or from the special-relativity
postulates, and this item by itself asserts no covariance under changes of
inertial frame.

Let $c>0$, let $k\ge2$ be an integer, let $\Omega\subseteq\mathbb R^3$ be an open set that is star-shaped with respect to a point $a\in\Omega$ ([[def-star-shaped-open-subset-of-rn]]), and let $I\subseteq\mathbb R$ be an interval with at least two elements ([[def-interval]]). Joint regularity on $\Omega\times I$ is read in the restriction convention of [[lem-em-joint-smooth-potentials]]: a map on $\Omega\times I$ is **jointly $C^m$** when it is the restriction of a $C^m$ map on some open neighbourhood of $\Omega\times I$ in $\mathbb R^4$. For open $I$ this is the ordinary open-domain class of [[def-ck-euclidean-maps-and-diffeomorphisms]] and agrees with the field class of [[def-em-fields]]; for non-open $I$ it is the convention that makes the statements below meaningful, and no time jet is asserted beyond the restricted values.

Let $E,B:\Omega\times I\to\mathbb R^3$ be jointly $C^k$ and satisfy the two source-free Maxwell equations of [[post-em-vacuum-maxwell]] pointwise on $\Omega\times I$:

$$\operatorname{div}B=0,\qquad\operatorname{curl}E=-\partial_tB,$$

with the divergence and curl of [[def-divergence-and-curl-of-a-c1-vector-field]] and the partial derivative $\partial_t$ at fixed position of [[def-directional-and-partial-derivatives]] (at included endpoints of a non-open $I$, as relative derivatives in the restriction convention). Then there are a scalar potential $\varphi:\Omega\times I\to\mathbb R$ that is jointly $C^{k-1}$ and a vector potential $A:\Omega\times I\to\mathbb R^3$ that is jointly $C^k$, both in the restriction convention, with

$$B=\operatorname{curl}A,\qquad E=-\nabla\varphi-\partial_tA\qquad\text{on }\Omega\times I,$$

so that $(\varphi,A)$ is a potential pair whose field pair is $(E,B)$, in the vocabulary of [[def-em-potential-gauge-and-field-conventions]]. If $E$ and $B$ are jointly $C^\infty$, then $\varphi$ and $A$ may be chosen jointly $C^\infty$. Conversely, if $\varphi$ and $A$ are jointly $C^\infty$ on $\Omega\times I$ in the restriction convention and $E:=-\nabla\varphi-\partial_tA$, $B:=\operatorname{curl}A$ are their field pair, then $\operatorname{div}B=0$ and $\operatorname{curl}E=-\partial_tB$ on $\Omega\times I$.

The theorem asserts existence on the stated star-shaped domain only: it claims no global potential on a general open set, no boundary, decay or growth condition on the potentials, and no uniqueness. Potentials are auxiliary objects of the framework and are not claimed to be observable.

A nonempty open set $U\subseteq\mathbb R^n$ is **star-shaped with respect to** $a\in U$ when

$$a+t(x-a)\in U\qquad\text{for every }x\in U\text{ and }0\le t\le1.$$

The point $a$ is a **star centre**. Every convex open set of [[def-convex-subset-of-euclidean-space]] is star-shaped with respect to each of its points. The nonemptiness and the chosen centre are part of the definition.

derivations.claim: The scalar witness is smooth and curl-free. On $U_1$ the denominator $x^2+y^2$ is strictly positive, so each component of $F$ is a quotient of smooth functions with nonvanishing denominator and $F$ is of class $C^\infty$ by [F6]. By [F7] the coordinates of $\operatorname{curl}F$ are the differences $\partial_yF_z-\partial_zF_y$, $\partial_zF_x-\partial_xF_z$ and $\partial_xF_y-\partial_yF_x$. The first two vanish because $F_z=0$ and the first two components of $F$ do not depend on $z$. For the third, the quotient rule of [F6] gives $\partial_xF_y=\partial_x\bigl(x/(x^2+y^2)\bigr)=\bigl((x^2+y^2)-2x^2\bigr)/(x^2+y^2)^2=(y^2-x^2)/(x^2+y^2)^2$ and $\partial_yF_x=\partial_y\bigl(-y/(x^2+y^2)\bigr)=-\bigl((x^2+y^2)-2y^2\bigr)/(x^2+y^2)^2=(y^2-x^2)/(x^2+y^2)^2$, so their difference is zero. Hence $\operatorname{curl}F=0$ on $U_1$.

The vector witness is smooth and divergence-free. On $U_2$ the norm $\lVert x\rVert_2$ is strictly positive, so $B$ is of class $C^\infty$ by [F6]. By [F7], $\operatorname{div}B=\sum_{i=1}^3\partial_i\bigl(x_i\lVert x\rVert_2^{-3}\bigr)$; the product and chain rules of [F6] together with $\partial_i\lVert x\rVert_2=x_i/\lVert x\rVert_2$ and the power rule of [F6] give $\partial_i\bigl(x_i\lVert x\rVert_2^{-3}\bigr)=\lVert x\rVert_2^{-3}+x_i\cdot(-3)\lVert x\rVert_2^{-4}\cdot x_i/\lVert x\rVert_2=\lVert x\rVert_2^{-3}-3x_i^2\lVert x\rVert_2^{-5}$. Summing over $i$ and using $\sum_ix_i^2=\lVert x\rVert_2^2$ yields $\operatorname{div}B=3\lVert x\rVert_2^{-3}-3\lVert x\rVert_2^{-5}\lVert x\rVert_2^{2}=0$.

The scalar domain is a connected open set. Let $p=(p_1,p_2,p_3)$ and $q=(q_1,q_2,q_3)$ be points of $U_1$; then $\rho_p:=\sqrt{p_1^2+p_2^2}>0$ and $\rho_q>0$. By the radial straight-line homotopy of [F11] applied in the plane, the maps $t\mapsto H_{\rho_p}(t):=\bigl((1-t)+t/\rho_p\bigr)(p_1,p_2)$ and $t\mapsto H_{\rho_q}(t)$ are continuous and never vanish, so they join $(p_1,p_2)$ to $u_p:=(p_1,p_2)/\rho_p$ and $(q_1,q_2)$ to $u_q$ in $\mathbb R^2\setminus\{0\}$; both $u_p,u_q$ lie on $S^1$, which is path-connected by [F11] applied with $n=2$, so fix a path $\sigma$ in $S^1$ from $u_p$ to $u_q$. The concatenation of the three paths $t\mapsto(H_{\rho_p}(t),p_3)$, $t\mapsto(\sigma(t),(1-t)p_3+tq_3)$ and $t\mapsto(H_{\rho_q}(1-t),q_3)$ is a path in $U_1$ from $p$ to $q$: the first two coordinates never vanish, because $H_{\rho_p}$ and $H_{\rho_q}$ take values in $\mathbb R^2\setminus\{0\}$ and $\sigma$ takes values in $S^1$, while the continuity of the three maps and of their concatenation follows from the continuity and finite-pasting suppliers in [F11]. Hence $U_1$ is path-connected by [F11], and therefore connected by [F11].

Basepoint reduction for loops in the punctured space. Let $\gamma_0$ be a based loop in $P$ at $x_0\in P$ and put $\rho:=\lVert x_0\rVert_2>0$. The maps $L(x):=x/\rho$ and $L^{-1}(x)=\rho x$ are linear maps of $\mathbb R^3$, hence bounded and continuous by [F11], and $L^{-1}\circ L=\mathrm{id}=L\circ L^{-1}$. If $L\circ\gamma_0$ is null-homotopic as a loop at $x_1:=x_0/\rho$, then composing that null-homotopy with the continuous map $L^{-1}$ gives a null-homotopy of $L^{-1}\circ L\circ\gamma_0=\gamma_0$; conversely composing a null-homotopy of $\gamma_0$ with $L$ gives one of $L\circ\gamma_0$. Hence a loop at $x_0$ is null-homotopic if and only if its image under $L$ is, and $x_1$ lies on the unit sphere $S^2$; it therefore suffices to treat loops based on $S^2$.

The circulation of the scalar witness. The map $\gamma(t)=(\cos t,\sin t,0)$, $t\in[0,2\pi]$, is a piecewise-$C^1$ path in $U_1$ by [F4], and $F$ is continuous on its trace. By the definition of the vector line integral in [F1], the integral along $\gamma$ is $\int_0^{2\pi}\langle F(\gamma(t)),\gamma'(t)\rangle\,dt$ with the derivative extension $\gamma'(t)=(-\sin t,\cos t,0)$ from [F4]. Since $x^2+y^2=\cos^2t+\sin^2t=1$ on the trace by the Pythagorean identity [F4], one has $F(\gamma(t))=(-\sin t,\cos t,0)$, so the integrand is $\langle(-\sin t,\cos t,0),(-\sin t,\cos t,0)\rangle=\sin^2t+\cos^2t=1$ by the inner product formula of [F9] and the Pythagorean identity [F4]. The fundamental theorem [F3] with $G(t)=t$ gives $\int_0^{2\pi}1\,dt=2\pi-0=2\pi$. The trace is the positively oriented unit circle by the parametrization statement of [F4].

The flux of the vector witness through the unit sphere. By [F4] the two parameter derivatives of $\Phi$ are $\Phi_\phi=(\cos\phi\cos\theta,\cos\phi\sin\theta,-\sin\phi)$ and $\Phi_\theta=(-\sin\phi\sin\theta,\sin\phi\cos\theta,0)$, computed with the derivative, chain and product rules of [F6]. By the coordinate formula for the cross product [F9], $\Phi_\phi\times\Phi_\theta=(\sin^2\phi\cos\theta,\ \sin^2\phi\sin\theta,\ \sin\phi\cos\phi)=\sin\phi\,\Phi$, using the Pythagorean identity [F4] in the third coordinate; since $\lVert\Phi\rVert_2=1$ by [F4], one has $B(\Phi)=\Phi/\lVert\Phi\rVert_2^3=\Phi$. Hence the integrand of the flux of [F8] is $\langle B(\Phi),\Phi_\phi\times\Phi_\theta\rangle=\sin\phi\,\langle\Phi,\Phi\rangle=\sin\phi$. The rectangle $D$ is a bounded Jordan set and the integrand is continuous, so [F10] applies and the section formula evaluates the flux as $\int_0^{2\pi}\bigl(\int_0^\pi\sin\phi\,d\phi\bigr)d\theta$; the fundamental theorem [F3] with $G=-\cos$ and the derivative of cosine [F4] gives $\int_0^\pi\sin\phi\,d\phi=-\cos\pi+\cos0=2$, so the flux is $\int_0^{2\pi}2\,d\theta=4\pi$. The patch $(D,\Phi)$ is admissible: on the interior of $D$ the cross product is nonzero (as $\sin\phi>0$ and $\Phi\ne0$ there) and the interior parametrization is injective, while the seam $\theta=0$ and $\theta=2\pi$ and the poles lie on the parameter boundary, all in the sense of [F8].

The two hemispheres as $C^2$ patches and their induced boundaries. The rectangles $D_N=[0,\pi/2]\times[0,2\pi]$ and $D_S=[\pi/2,\pi]\times[0,2\pi]$ are Type I and Type II regions, hence elementary Green regions with their positive boundary chains in the sense of [F8], and the restrictions of $\Phi$ to them are $C^2$ on an open neighbourhood with cross product nonzero on the parameter interior and no interior image shared with a distinct parameter point, while poles and seam identifications lie only on the boundary, so they are $C^2$ patches over finite elementary Green regions with induced boundary chains as in [F8]. For a rectangle $[a,b]\times[c,d]$ the positive boundary chain runs along the lower graph from left to right, up the right side, back along the upper graph and down the left side [F8]. Under $\Phi$ and using the periods of sine and cosine from [F5], the lower and upper graphs have the same image, namely the meridian $\phi\mapsto(\sin\phi,0,\cos\phi)$ on $[a,b]$, traversed in opposite directions; the left side of $D_N$ lies at $\phi=0$, where $\Phi(0,\theta)=(0,0,1)$ is constant, and the right side of $D_S$ lies at $\phi=\pi$, where $\Phi(\pi,\theta)=(0,0,-1)$ is constant; the right side of $D_N$ and the left side of $D_S$ both equal the equator $\theta\mapsto(\cos\theta,\sin\theta,0)$, traversed in the positive and in the reverse direction respectively. Thus the north induced boundary chain consists of a meridian arc, the equator, the reversed meridian arc and a degenerate polar arc, and the south induced boundary chain consists of a meridian arc, a degenerate polar arc, the reversed meridian arc and the reversed equator.

The radial deformation to the unit sphere. By [F11] the map $H(x,t)=\bigl((1-t)+t/\lVert x\rVert_2\bigr)x$ is continuous on $P\times[0,1]$, satisfies $H(x,1)=x/\lVert x\rVert_2=\rho(x)$, and fixes every point of $S^2$ for all $t$. Let $\gamma_0$ be a based loop at a point $x_1\in S^2$; then $(s,t)\mapsto H(\gamma_0(s),t)$ is continuous by [F11], equal to $\gamma_0(s)$ at $t=0$, equal to $\rho\circ\gamma_0$ at $t=1$, and constant equal to $x_1$ along the basepoint for every $t$; hence it is a path homotopy from $\gamma_0$ to the loop $\rho\circ\gamma_0$, which takes values in $S^2$ by [F11]. In the vocabulary of [F11] this says that $\gamma_0$ and $\rho\circ\gamma_0$ are path-homotopic loops at $x_1$.

No global $C^2$ scalar potential on $U_1$. Suppose $\phi:U_1\to\mathbb R$ were $C^2$ with $F=\nabla\phi$, exactness in the sense of [F2]. Since $\phi$ is $C^1$ and $\gamma$ is a piecewise-$C^1$ path in $U_1$, the gradient theorem of [F1] gives $\int_\gamma F\cdot d\mathbf r=\phi(\gamma(2\pi))-\phi(\gamma(0))$. By the periodicity of sine and cosine from [F5] and the values at zero from [F4], $\gamma(2\pi)=(\cos 2\pi,\sin 2\pi,0)=(1,0,0)=\gamma(0)$, so the right-hand side is zero, whereas step 1.5 computed the same integral as $2\pi\ne0$, a contradiction. Hence no such $\phi$ exists on $U_1$, while $U_1$ is a connected open set by step 1.3.

No global $C^1$ vector potential on $U_2$. Suppose $A$ were a $C^1$ field on the open set $U_2$ with $\operatorname{curl}A=B$, a vector potential in the sense of [F2]. The image of each closed hemisphere under $\Phi$ is contained in $S^2\subseteq U_2$, and $A$ is $C^1$ on the open set $U_2$ containing it, so the classical Stokes theorem of [F8] applies to the two $C^2$ patches of step 1.7 and gives, with the flux of [F8], $\oint_{\Phi(\partial D_N)}A\cdot d\mathbf r=\int_{D_N}\langle(\operatorname{curl}A)\circ\Phi,\Phi_\phi\times\Phi_\theta\rangle$ and the analogous identity over $D_S$. Replacing $\operatorname{curl}A$ by $B$, the right-hand sides are the fluxes of $B$ over the two hemispheres, whose sum is the total flux $4\pi$ of step 1.6 because the two patches share only the boundary seam and together cover the sphere in the same orientation. On the left-hand sides, the induced boundary chains of step 1.7 have the structure described there: in the north chain the two meridian arcs have the same image with opposite orientations, so their integrals cancel by reversal [F1], and the degenerate polar arc has constant image, so its integral is zero [F1]; the north circulation therefore equals the equator integral, and the south circulation equals the reverse equator integral by the same cancellation, so their sum is zero. Adding the two Stokes identities then gives $0=4\pi$, a contradiction; hence no such $A$ exists.

The unit sphere loop is null-homotopic in the unit sphere. Let $\gamma_0$ be a based loop at $x_1\in S^2$. The sphere $S^2$ is simply connected by [F11] (applied with $n=2$), so by the definition of simple connectedness in [F11] its fundamental group at $x_1$ has exactly one element; by the vocabulary of based loops and fundamental groups in [F11] this means that the class of the loop $\rho\circ\gamma_0$ equals the class of the constant loop, that is, there is a path homotopy in $S^2$ from $\rho\circ\gamma_0$ to the constant loop at $x_1$.

The punctured space is simply connected. First, $P$ is path-connected: for $x\in P$ the radial homotopy of [F11] gives a continuous path $t\mapsto H(x,t)$ from $x$ to $\rho(x)\in S^2$ that stays in $P$, the sphere $S^2$ is path-connected by [F11] (applied with $n=3$), and concatenating a radial path, a path in $S^2$ and a reversed radial path gives a path between any two points, with continuity and concatenation as in [F11]. Now let $\gamma_0$ be a based loop at $x_0\in P$. By step 1.4 it suffices to treat the case $x_0=x_1\in S^2$; in that case step 1.8 gives a path homotopy in $P$ from $\gamma_0$ to $\rho\circ\gamma_0$, and step 2.3 gives a path homotopy in $S^2$ from $\rho\circ\gamma_0$ to the constant loop, which, composed with the inclusion $S^2\subseteq P$, is a path homotopy in $P$; by the equivalence-relation property of path homotopy in [F11] the loop $\gamma_0$ is path-homotopic to the constant loop, so every based loop of $P$ is null-homotopic and the fundamental group of $P$ at every basepoint has exactly one element. Since $P$ is nonempty and path-connected, [F11] makes it simply connected.

Conclusion and scope. Step 1.1 and step 2.1 together say that $U_1$ is a connected open set carrying a $C^\infty$ field $F$ with $\operatorname{curl}F=0$ that is not the gradient of any $C^2$ function; step 1.2 and step 2.2 say that on the open set $U_2$ the $C^\infty$ field $B$ satisfies $\operatorname{div}B=0$ while admitting no $C^1$ vector potential; and step 3.1 shows that the domain of the second obstruction is simply connected, so simple connectivity is not sufficient for a vector potential. A pair defined on a set of the form $\mathbb R^3\times[t_0,T]$ with $t_0<T$ is of class $C^k$, $k\ge1$, **in the extension sense** when there are an open interval $J\supset[t_0,T]$ and a potential pair of class $C^k$ on the open set $\mathbb R^3\times J$ whose restriction to $\mathbb R^3\times[t_0,T]$ the given pair is; the same wording is used for $C^\infty$ and for the single functions $\varphi$ and $\chi$ below.
