**Vector witness.** Let $U\subseteq\mathbb R^3$ be open and star-shaped with centre $a\in U$ ([[def-star-shaped-open-subset-of-rn]]), let $I\subseteq\mathbb R$ be an interval, let $k\ge1$, and let $B:U\times I\to\mathbb R^3$ be jointly $C^k$ with $\operatorname{div}B(\cdot,t)=0$ on $U$ for every $t\in I$ ([[def-divergence-and-curl-of-a-c1-vector-field]]). Then

$$A(x,t):=\int_0^1s\,B\bigl(a+s(x-a),t\bigr)\times(x-a)\,ds$$

is jointly $C^k$ on $U\times I$ and

$$\operatorname{curl}A(\cdot,t)=B(\cdot,t)\qquad(t\in I),$$

the curl being taken in the spatial variables and the cross product being that of [[def-cross-product-in-r3]].

**Scalar witness.** If in addition $C:U\times I\to\mathbb R^3$ is jointly $C^k$ with $\operatorname{curl}C(\cdot,t)=0$ on $U$ for every $t\in I$, then

$$\phi(x,t):=-\int_0^1\bigl\langle C\bigl(a+s(x-a),t\bigr),\,x-a\bigr\rangle\,ds$$

is jointly $C^k$ on $U\times I$ and

$$\nabla\phi(\cdot,t)=-C(\cdot,t)\qquad(t\in I),$$

the gradient and inner product being those of [[def-directional-and-partial-derivatives]] and [[def-euclidean-inner-product]]. For jointly $C^\infty$ data both potentials are jointly $C^\infty$. No global potential on a non-star-shaped open set is claimed, and the restrictions are continuous at included endpoints by joint regularity.

Let the laboratory region $U\cong I\times\Omega$, its spatial Euclidean structure
and its units be those of [[def-em-lab-geometry]] and
[[def-em-si-conventions]], and let $k\ge1$. An **electric field of class
$C^k$** on the region is a map $E:\Omega\times I\to\mathbb R^3$ that is of class
$C^k$ in the sense of [[def-ck-euclidean-maps-and-diffeomorphisms]]; a
**magnetic field of class $C^k$** is a map $B:\Omega\times I\to\mathbb R^3$ of
the same class. At fixed $t\in I$ the maps $E(\cdot,t),B(\cdot,t):\Omega\to
\mathbb R^3$ are real spatial vector fields on the region $\Omega$, read in the
$\delta$-orthonormal basis $(e_1,e_2,e_3)$ of the frame. The framework uses:
$C^1$ fields in the classical Maxwell branch, $C^2$ fields where second or
mixed time-space derivatives of the fields appear, and $C^\infty$ fields in
the smooth existence branches; every statement carries its own regularity and
no regularity beyond it is asserted.

Conventions:

(a) The **polar-vector** and **axial-vector** conventions mean the following
component rules under a spatial orthogonal coordinate change $y'=Qy$, where
$Q$ is a real $3\times3$ matrix with $Q^{\mathsf T}Q=I_3$. Transpose,
matrix product and identity are those of [[def-transpose-of-a-matrix]] and
[[def-matrix-product-and-identity-matrix]], and $\det Q$ is the determinant
of [[def-determinant-of-a-square-matrix]]. At corresponding
points $E'(y',t)=QE(y,t)$ and $B'(y',t)=(\det Q)QB(y,t)$. Thus polar and axial
components agree in their transformation rule when $\det Q=1$ and differ by
a sign when $\det Q=-1$. These rules specify the orientation convention;
the adopted inertial descriptions have positive orientation, and no physical
orientation-reversing change of description is adopted here.

(b) The fields are defined by their values on $\Omega\times I$, and no value at
a point of singular source support is asserted.

(c) $E$ carries V m$^{-1}$ and $B$ carries T.

(d) The identification of the pair $(E,B)$ with the components of an
alternating two-form, including its transformation behaviour, is made in the
framework's electromagnetic two-form definition on this page and is not
presupposed here.

Let the laboratory region and its chart be those of [[def-em-lab-geometry]], with
the units of [[def-em-si-conventions]].

(a) [Charge parameter] The framework takes a real **charge parameter**
$q\in\mathbb R$, measured in coulombs, attached to a source; its sign is the
sign of the source and it is a parameter of the model. Charge quantisation is
not asserted.

(b) [Smooth source fields] A **smooth (volume) source field** on
$\Omega\times I$ is a pair $(\rho,J)$ of maps $\rho:\Omega\times I\to\mathbb R$,
$J:\Omega\times I\to\mathbb R^3$ that is continuous on $\Omega\times I$ and of
class $C^1$ wherever a displayed equation differentiates it; $\rho$ is the
**frame charge density** (C m$^{-3}$) and $J$ the **frame current density**
(A m$^{-2}$). For each fixed $t\in I$ retain the compact Jordan branch: if
$V\subseteq\Omega$ is compact and Jordan measurable, define

$$Q_R(V,t):=\int_V\rho(y,t)dy$$

by [[def-riemann-integral-over-a-jordan-set]], with integrability supplied by
[[thm-continuous-functions-on-compact-jordan-sets-are-integrable]]. For the
full measurable-volume branch assume Countable Choice ([[def-countable-choice]]),
as required by the published Lebesgue-measure interface. If $V$ is any bounded
Lebesgue-measurable subset with compact closure $\overline V\subseteq\Omega$,
define

$$Q(V,t):=\int_V\rho(y,t)d\lambda_3(y)=\int_{\mathbb R^3}F_t(y)\mathbf{1}_V(y)d\lambda_3(y),$$

where $F_t=\rho(\cdot,t)$ on $\Omega$ and $0$ elsewhere; the signed integral is
defined through its positive and negative parts
([[def-integral-over-a-measurable-set]],
[[def-integrable-real-and-complex-functions-and-their-integrals]]). The
function $F_t$ is Borel, and hence Lebesgue measurable: for every open
$O\subseteq\mathbb R$ its preimage inside the open set $\Omega$ is relatively
open in $\Omega$, hence open in $\mathbb R^3$, and the closed complement of
$\Omega$ is added precisely when $0\in O$
([[thm-continuous-preimages-of-borel-sets-are-borel]],
[[thm-borel-sets-are-lebesgue-measurable]]). This integral is absolutely
finite: $\rho(\cdot,t)$ is bounded on the compact $\overline V$ by
[[thm-extreme-value-metric]], $V$ has finite Lebesgue measure by
[[prop-lebesgue-measure-is-sigma-finite-and-finite-on-bounded-sets]], and the
monotonicity and homogeneity of the nonnegative integral
([[prop-order-and-scalar-rules-for-the-nonnegative-integral]]) bound
$\int|F_t|\mathbf{1}_Vd\lambda_3\le M_t\lambda_3(V)<\infty$, the indicator
integral being its simple-function value
([[prop-the-nonnegative-integral-agrees-with-the-simple-integral]]); the
positive and negative parts are measurable by
[[prop-closure-properties-of-measurable-functions-used-by-the-integral]]. On
the compact Jordan branch, under the same Countable Choice assumption,
$Q=Q_R$ by [[lem-riemann-lebesgue-comparison-for-distribution-test-integrands]].
The
empty region has charge zero in both branches. The current flux remains
defined independently: for each oriented surface patch in $\Omega$ the current
flux at time $t$ is the surface integral of $J(\cdot,t)$ in the induced
orientation, as defined in [[def-oriented-unit-normal-and-flux-of-a-surface-patch]].
Point sources and sheet sources are not source fields in this sense; they are
different objects, defined by their own pairings when the framework uses them.

(c) [Covariant identification] Write $j:=(c\rho,J)$, so $j^0=c\rho$ and
$j^i=J^i$. The framework adopts as a model premise the identification of the
charge-current of a source with a vector field of the affine Minkowski model,
and hence the component transformation law of
[[thm-sr-tensor-and-current-transformation]] for $j$ between inertial charts.
This is a model premise, not a theorem about physical currents.

(d) [Frame density, scalar multiplier and the normalized material branch]
Suppose additionally that the identified $j$ is $C^1$ and $j=\rho_0U$, with a
$C^1$ future timelike vector field $U$ and a $C^1$ real scalar multiplier
$\rho_0$. Since $U^0>0$, define the normalized chart direction $u:=U/U^0$, so
$u^0=1$, $u^i=U^i/U^0$. Then $j=(\rho_0U^0)u$ and, because the electromagnetic
convention is $j^0=c\rho$,

$$\rho=\rho_0U^0/c,\qquad J^i=\rho_0U^i=c\rho\,u^i.$$

Pointwise equality $\rho=\rho_0$ holds if and only if $\rho_0(U^0-c)=0$,
including the zero-multiplier case. Where $\rho_0\ne0$, equality is equivalent
to $U^0=c$, which does not alone imply $U^i=0$ for an arbitrary future timelike
$U$. Thus a scalar multiplier is not automatically a Lorentz rest charge
density. The direction $u$ is chart normalized, with no unit or
proper-four-velocity normalization imposed in this general branch; if its
coordinate velocity interpretation is adopted, the spatial velocity is
$v^i:=cu^i$.

For the separate convective source model, explicitly assume that $U$ is the
material proper-time four-velocity, normalized by $\eta(U,U)=-c^2$ as in
[[thm-sr-proper-time-and-observer-decomposition]]. This is an additional model
condition, not a consequence of the factorization $j=\rho_0U$. In that branch,
$U=\gamma(c,v)$, $|v|<c$, $\gamma=(1-|v|^2/c^2)^{-1/2}$, and

$$\rho=\gamma\rho_0,\qquad J=\rho v.$$

Here $\rho_0$ is the rest charge density of this stipulated convective model:
in a comoving inertial frame $U=(c,0,0,0)$ and $j=(c\rho_0,0,0,0)$. The
equality $\rho=\rho_0$ then holds exactly where $\rho_0=0$ or $v=0$
(equivalently $\gamma=1$). Both signs of charge and the zero-density case are
retained.

(e) [Scope] This definition fixes the source objects of the smooth branch and
their transformation interface. It asserts no conservation law (that is proved
for stated source classes) and no regularity of singular sources.

Let $n\ge1$, let $U\subseteq\mathbb R^n$ be open, let $F,G:U\to\mathbb R^n$ be $C^1$, let $f:U\to\mathbb R$ be $C^1$ and let $a,b\in\mathbb R$. Then $aF+bG$ and $fF$ are $C^1$ on $U$ and

$$\operatorname{div}(aF+bG)=a\operatorname{div}F+b\operatorname{div}G,$$

$$\operatorname{div}(fF)=\langle\nabla f,F\rangle+f\operatorname{div}F.$$

If moreover $n=3$, then

$$\operatorname{curl}(aF+bG)=a\operatorname{curl}F+b\operatorname{curl}G,\qquad \operatorname{curl}(fF)=\nabla f\times F+f\operatorname{curl}F.$$

Here $\operatorname{div}$, $\operatorname{curl}$ and the coordinate naming are those of [[def-divergence-and-curl-of-a-c1-vector-field]], $\nabla f$ is the gradient of [[def-jacobian-matrix-and-gradient]], $\langle\cdot,\cdot\rangle$ is the inner product of [[def-euclidean-inner-product]] and $\times$ is the cross product of [[def-cross-product-in-r3]].

Let $U\subseteq\mathbb R^m$, $a\in U$, $v\in\mathbb R^m$, and $f:U\to\mathbb R^n$. If the line map $t\mapsto f(a+tv)$ is defined near $0$, its derivative at $0$ is the **directional derivative**

$$D_vf(a):=\lim_{t\to0}\frac{f(a+tv)-f(a)}{t}.$$

For a standard basis vector $e_j$ ([[lem-standard-basis-of-f-n]]), $D_{e_j}f(a)$ is the **$j$th partial derivative**, written $\partial_jf(a)$. These are ordinary vector-valued one-variable derivatives in the sense of [[def-vector-valued-derivative-and-integral]].

Let $A \subseteq \mathbb{R}$, let $c \in A$ be a limit point of $A$
([[def-limit-point-r]]), let $f, g : A \to \mathbb{R}$ be differentiable at $c$
([[def-derivative]]) and let $\alpha \in \mathbb{R}$. Then:

1. $f + g$ is differentiable at $c$ and $(f+g)'(c) = f'(c) + g'(c)$;
2. $\alpha f$ is differentiable at $c$ and $(\alpha f)'(c) = \alpha f'(c)$;
3. $fg$ is differentiable at $c$ and $(fg)'(c) = f'(c)g(c) + f(c)g'(c)$;
4. if $g(c) \ne 0$ then, writing $A_0 := \{\, x \in A : g(x) \ne 0 \,\}$, the
   point $c$ lies in $A_0$ and is a limit point of $A_0$, the quotient
   $(f/g)|_{A_0} : A_0 \to \mathbb{R}$, $x \mapsto f(x)/g(x)$, is differentiable
   at $c$ as a function on $A_0$, and
   $$\bigl((f/g)|_{A_0}\bigr)'(c) \;=\; \frac{f'(c)\,g(c) - f(c)\,g'(c)}{g(c)^{2}} .$$

Each claim asserts two things: that the derivative on the left exists, and that
it has the stated value. Both are proved.

**Why claim 4 is stated on $A_0$.** The function $f/g$ is not defined where $g$
vanishes, and $g$ may vanish at points of $A$ far from $c$; restricting to $A_0$
is forced. That the restriction still has $c$ as a limit point, so that a
derivative there means anything at all, is not free either, and it is the last
claim of [[lem-sign-preservation-near-a-limit]] applied to $g$. The hypothesis
is $g(c) \ne 0$, not "$g$ vanishes nowhere".

**Everything is proved through
[[thm-caratheodory-characterisation]].** No difference quotient is estimated and
no limit theorem beyond continuity is used, so no choice principle is spent.
The four identities are four algebraic rearrangements of an increment, each
followed by a reading of [[thm-algebra-of-continuous-functions]].
If $f$ is $C^2$ on an open subset of $\mathbb R^m$, then $\partial_i\partial_j f=\partial_j\partial_i f$ for every pair of coordinate indices.

Let $U\subseteq\mathbb R^3$ be open and let $F:U\to\mathbb R^3$ be $C^2$. Then $\operatorname{curl}\operatorname{curl}F$, $\nabla\operatorname{div}F$ and $\Delta F$ are all defined on $U$ and

$$\operatorname{curl}\operatorname{curl}F=\nabla\operatorname{div}F-\Delta F.$$

Here $\Delta F$ is the componentwise Laplacian of [[def-laplacian-of-a-c2-function]].

Let $n\ge1$, let $U\subseteq\mathbb R^n$ be open and let $f:U\to\mathbb R$ be $C^2$ in the sense of [[def-ck-and-multi-index-notation-in-several-variables]]. Then $\nabla f$ is a $C^1$ field on $U$ by [[def-ck-euclidean-maps-and-diffeomorphisms]], since each of its components $\partial_if$ has continuous first partial derivatives, so its divergence is defined; the **Laplacian** of $f$ is

$$\Delta f:=\operatorname{div}\nabla f=\sum_{i<n}\partial_i\partial_if,$$

with the gradient of [[def-jacobian-matrix-and-gradient]] and the divergence of [[def-divergence-and-curl-of-a-c1-vector-field]]. A $C^2$ function with $\Delta f=0$ on $U$ is called **harmonic** on $U$.

For a $C^2$ map $F=(F_0,\ldots,F_{q-1}):U\to\mathbb R^q$, whose components are $C^2$ by [[def-ck-euclidean-maps-and-diffeomorphisms]], $\Delta F$ is the field whose $i$th coordinate is $\Delta F_i$. In the three-coordinate naming of this page, $\Delta f=\partial_x\partial_xf+\partial_y\partial_yf+\partial_z\partial_zf$ and $\Delta F=(\Delta F_x,\Delta F_y,\Delta F_z)$.

Let $U\subseteq\mathbb R^3$ be open and let $F:U\to\mathbb R^3$ be $C^2$. Then $\operatorname{curl}F$ is a $C^1$ field on $U$ and

$$\operatorname{div}(\operatorname{curl}F)=0\qquad\text{on }U.$$

Let $U\subseteq\mathbb R^3$ be open and let $\phi:U\to\mathbb R$ be $C^2$. Then $\nabla\phi$ is a $C^1$ field on $U$ and

$$\operatorname{curl}\nabla\phi=0\qquad\text{on }U.$$

Adopt as a physical postulate of this framework the following four equations for
the fields of [[def-em-fields]] and the sources of [[def-em-sources]] on the
laboratory region $U\cong I\times\Omega$ of [[def-em-lab-geometry]], with
$\mu_0>0$, $c>0$, $\varepsilon_0=(\mu_0c^2)^{-1}$ and the SI units of
[[def-em-si-conventions]].

(a) [Smooth branch] Let $E,B$ be jointly $C^1$ fields with the additional
derivatives required by each equation existing and continuous, and let
$\rho,J$ be continuous. Then, with the divergence and curl of
[[def-divergence-and-curl-of-a-c1-vector-field]] and the partial derivative
$\partial_t$ at fixed position of
[[def-directional-and-partial-derivatives]],

$$\operatorname{div}E=\rho/\varepsilon_0,\qquad \operatorname{div}B=0,\qquad \operatorname{curl}E=-\partial_tB,\qquad \operatorname{curl}B=\mu_0J+c^{-2}\partial_tE.$$

(b) [Weak branch] Let instead $E,B$ be locally integrable $\mathbb R^3$-valued
fields and $\rho,J$ locally integrable scalar and vector fields on
$I\times\Omega$, identified with their regular distributions
([[def-regular-distribution-from-a-locally-integrable-function]],
[[thm-locally-integrable-functions-embed-in-distributions]]). Let
$\operatorname{div}$, $\operatorname{curl}$ and $\partial_t$ act as
distributional derivatives, componentwise, and let $\psi$ range over
$C_c^\infty(I\times\Omega)$ ([[def-test-function-space-d-of-an-open-set]]).
Then the same four identities hold in the sense of [[def-distribution]]: the
pairings

$$\langle\operatorname{div}E-\rho/\varepsilon_0,\psi\rangle,\qquad \langle\operatorname{div}B,\psi\rangle,\qquad \langle\operatorname{curl}E+\partial_tB,\psi\rangle,\qquad \langle\operatorname{curl}B-\mu_0J-c^{-2}\partial_tE,\psi\rangle$$

all vanish for every such $\psi$, all derivatives being distributional
derivatives ([[def-distributional-derivative]]).

(c) [Scope] The postulate contains no magnetic charge: $\operatorname{div}B=0$
and no magnetic-source term appears in $\operatorname{curl}E$. Sources that
are not locally integrable functions (point or sheet sources) are covered by
neither branch and require their own definition. The equations are adopted
classical vacuum physics in the named inertial chart; they are not deduced from
charge conservation, from empirical agreement or from the special-relativity
postulates, and this item by itself asserts no covariance under changes of
inertial frame.

Let $c>0$, let $\Omega\subseteq\mathbb R^3$ be open, let $I\subseteq\mathbb R$ be an interval with at least two elements ([[def-interval]]), let $k\ge2$ be an integer, let $(\varphi,A)$ be a potential pair of class $C^k$ jointly on $\Omega\times I$ and let $\chi$ be a gauge function of class $C^k$ jointly on $\Omega\times I$, all in the conventions of [[def-em-potential-gauge-and-field-conventions]] and [[def-em-gauge-transformation]]: $E(\varphi,A)=-\nabla\varphi-\partial_tA$, $B(\varphi,A)=\operatorname{curl}A$ and $T_\chi(\varphi,A)=(\varphi-\partial_t\chi,\ A+\nabla\chi)$; for a non-open $I$ the joint $C^k$ classes are read in the open-neighbourhood restriction convention of [[lem-em-joint-smooth-potentials]] (for open $I$ this is the ordinary class of [[def-ck-euclidean-maps-and-diffeomorphisms]]).

Then $T_\chi(\varphi,A)$ is a potential pair of class $C^{k-1}$ jointly on $\Omega\times I$ and its field pair is the field pair of $(\varphi,A)$:

$$E(T_\chi(\varphi,A))=E(\varphi,A),\qquad B(T_\chi(\varphi,A))=B(\varphi,A)\qquad\text{on }\Omega\times I,$$

the common values being maps $\Omega\times I\to\mathbb R^3$ of class $C^{k-1}$ jointly, that is, fields of the framework in the sense of [[def-em-fields]]. In particular gauge related potential representations of one field pair have equal field pairs: the electric and magnetic fields are gauge invariants of the framework, and no value of $\varphi$, of $A$ or of $\chi$ is asserted to be observable.

The proof uses only the defining formulas, the vanishing of $\operatorname{curl}\nabla\chi$ for the $C^2$ function $\chi$ and the equality of the time-space mixed partials $\partial_t\partial_i\chi=\partial_i\partial_t\chi$; no Maxwell equation, no hypothesis on $\Omega$ beyond openness, and no choice principle is used.

Let $c>0$, let $U\cong I\times\Omega$ be the laboratory region of [[def-em-lab-geometry]] with its restricted inertial chart, let fields and units be those of [[def-em-fields]] and [[def-em-si-conventions]], and let the scalar-vector potential vocabulary on that region be that of [[def-em-potential-gauge-and-field-conventions]]: a **potential pair** $(\varphi,A)$ of class $C^k$ on $\Omega\times I$ consists of $\varphi:\Omega\times I\to\mathbb R$ and $A:\Omega\times I\to\mathbb R^3$ of class $C^k$ jointly in the sense of [[def-ck-euclidean-maps-and-diffeomorphisms]], and for a non-open time interval $I$ the joint classes in this item are read in the open-neighbourhood restriction convention of [[lem-em-joint-smooth-potentials]] (for open $I$ this is the ordinary class of [[def-ck-euclidean-maps-and-diffeomorphisms]]); for $k\ge1$ the **field pair** is

$$E(\varphi,A):=-\nabla\varphi-\partial_tA,\qquad B(\varphi,A):=\operatorname{curl}A,$$

where $\nabla$ is the gradient, $\operatorname{div}$ and $\operatorname{curl}$ are those of [[def-divergence-and-curl-of-a-c1-vector-field]], and $\partial_t$ is the partial derivative at fixed position of [[def-directional-and-partial-derivatives]]. For $k\ge1$ the **Lorenz divergence** of the pair is $G(\varphi,A):=\operatorname{div}A+c^{-2}\partial_t\varphi$. The definitions in this item are stated on the laboratory region; the framework's fields are those of [[def-em-fields]], and no field equation is assumed anywhere below.

(a) [Representations] Let $k\ge2$ be an integer and let $(E,B)$ be a field pair of class $C^{k-1}$ on $\Omega\times I$, meaning $E,B:\Omega\times I\to\mathbb R^3$ of class $C^{k-1}$ jointly as in [[def-em-fields]]. A **potential representation of class $C^k$** of $(E,B)$ is a potential pair $(\varphi,A)$ of class $C^k$ on $\Omega\times I$ whose field pair is $(E,B)$, that is, $E=-\nabla\varphi-\partial_tA$ and $B=\operatorname{curl}A$ on $\Omega\times I$. More generally, a potential pair of class $C^1$ represents a specified field pair whenever these two identities hold, even if the fields have greater regularity than the defining derivatives alone guarantee. This definition asserts neither existence nor uniqueness. On a star-shaped spatial region [[pthm-em-spacetime-potentials]] supplies $\varphi\in C^{r-1}$ and $A\in C^r$ for jointly $C^r$ field data, $r\ge2$, and smooth potentials for smooth data; it does not assert a $C^r$ scalar potential for merely $C^r$ data. Equality of field pairs does not by itself assert gauge relatedness on an arbitrary region; a converse needs its own domain and regularity hypotheses.

(b) [Gauge functions and gauge equivalence] A **gauge function** of class $C^m$, $m\ge2$, on $\Omega\times I$ is a function $\chi:\Omega\times I\to\mathbb R$ of class $C^m$ jointly; its **gauge transformation** sends a potential pair $(\varphi,A)$ of class $C^m$ to

$$T_\chi(\varphi,A):=(\varphi-\partial_t\chi,\ A+\nabla\chi),$$

a potential pair of class $C^{m-1}$. Two potential pairs are **gauge related** when one is the gauge transform of the other by some gauge function. On pairs and generators of class $C^\infty$, $T_0$ is the identity and $T_{\chi_1}\bigl(T_{\chi_2}(\varphi,A)\bigr)=T_{\chi_1+\chi_2}(\varphi,A)$ for all $C^\infty$ generators $\chi_1,\chi_2$; hence gauge relatedness is an equivalence relation on the $C^\infty$ potential pairs, the inverse of $T_\chi$ being $T_{-\chi}$. For a fixed finite class the transform drops one order, and relatedness is used only through the transform it records.

(c) [Conditions] A potential pair is **in Lorenz gauge** on $\Omega\times I$ when $G(\varphi,A)=\operatorname{div}A+c^{-2}\partial_t\varphi=0$ throughout $\Omega\times I$, and **in Coulomb gauge** in the chosen spatial chart when $\operatorname{div}A=0$ throughout $\Omega\times I$. These are properties of a pair in the stated conventions. The existence of a gauge function achieving either condition, with or without prescribed initial or boundary data, is a separate PDE conclusion with its own hypotheses and is not asserted by this definition.

(d) [Physical status] The physical content of a representation is its field pair $(E,B)$ of [[def-em-fields]]; the values of $\varphi$, of $A$ and of any gauge function are convention dependent and are auxiliary, and gauge related representations have the same field pair. The scalar potential $\varphi$ carries the volt, the vector potential $A$ carries the tesla metre, and a gauge function carries V s $=$ T m$^2$, so its time derivative and gradient have the units of $\varphi$ and $A$, respectively, consistently with [[def-em-si-conventions]]. No value of $\varphi$ or $A$ is by itself an observable or evidence for a field.

For the potential pair, $\operatorname{div}B=\operatorname{div}\operatorname{curl}A=0$ by [F7], and $\operatorname{curl}E=\operatorname{curl}(-\nabla\varphi-\partial_tA)=-\operatorname{curl}\nabla\varphi-\operatorname{curl}\partial_tA$ by linearity [F4]; the first term vanishes by [F7] applied to the $C^2$ function $\varphi$, and the second equals $\partial_t\operatorname{curl}A=\partial_tB$ by the componentwise commutation [F5], so $\operatorname{curl}E=-\partial_tB$ on $\Omega\times I$.

Equivalence with the sourced system. By [F8] the sourced Maxwell equations for $(E,B,\rho,J)$ are the four identities $\operatorname{div}E=\rho/\varepsilon_0$, $\operatorname{div}B=0$, $\operatorname{curl}E=-\partial_tB$ and $\operatorname{curl}B=\mu_0J+c^{-2}\partial_tE$ on $\Omega\times I$; the pair $(E,B)$ is of class $C^1$ by step 1.1 with all derivatives required by those equations existing and continuous, and $\rho,J$ are continuous by [F3]. The second and third identities hold identically by step 2.3. The first is equivalent, by step 2.1, to $W\varphi-\partial_tG=\rho/\varepsilon_0$, and the fourth is equivalent, by step 2.2, to $WA+\nabla G=\mu_0J$. Hence the sourced Maxwell equations hold for $(E,B,\rho,J)$ if and only if the two residual equations of (a) hold.

Residual generators. If in addition to $G=0$ the gauge function satisfies $W\chi=0$ on $\Omega\times I$, then step 2.4 gives $G(T_\chi(\varphi,A))=G-W\chi=0$, so the transformed pair is again in Lorenz gauge, and by [F9] it has the same field pair. For nonempty $\Omega$, take $\chi(x,t)=x_1$: all its second partial derivatives vanish, hence $W\chi=0$, while $\partial_t\chi=0$ and $\nabla\chi=(1,0,0)$, so $T_\chi(\varphi,A)=(\varphi,A+(1,0,0))$ is distinct from $(\varphi,A)$ on the nonempty product. Thus the Lorenz condition does not determine the pair on a nonempty region. On empty $\Omega$ all identities are vacuous and there is only one potential pair.

Decoupling under the Lorenz condition. Assume additionally $G=0$ on $\Omega\times I$. Then the $C^1$ function $G$ has $\partial_tG=0$ and $\nabla G=0$ on $\Omega\times I$ by [F4]: each spatial restriction is identically zero, and the time restriction is identically zero on the nondegenerate interval $I$, so its interior and relative endpoint difference quotients vanish. Hence the residual equations of step 3.1 read $W\varphi=\rho/\varepsilon_0$ and $WA=\mu_0J$ there; conversely, if these two wave equations hold then the residual equations hold and, by step 3.1, the sourced Maxwell system holds for the pair. This equivalence is asserted only under the explicitly imposed hypothesis $G=0$: for a general representative the equivalent conditions are the residual equations of step 3.1, which contain the derivatives $\partial_tG$ and $\nabla G$ of the representative's own Lorenz divergence, and no step infers $G=0$ from the Maxwell equations.

Conclusion and scope. Step 2.1 and step 2.2 give the exact pointwise identities of (a), and step 3.1 identifies the two residual equations with the sourced Maxwell system; step 2.3 records the two automatic source-free equations. Step 2.4 gives the gauge shift and the equivalence of the Lorenz condition for the transform with $W\chi=G$; step 4.1 gives the decoupling inside $G=0$, with the explicit warning that Maxwell alone does not impose that condition; and step 3.2 gives the residual generators. Throughout, no existence of a solution of $W\chi=G$ or of a generator with prescribed data is asserted, no boundary, decay or initial condition is imposed, and $C^2$ is the exact standing regularity: for a merely $C^1$ pair the expressions $W\varphi$, $WA$, $\Delta$ and $\partial_tG$ of the Statement need not exist. No choice principle is used, and no hypothesis is made on the shape of $\Omega$ beyond openness.

citations.quote:
Let $c>0$ and let $\Omega\subseteq\mathbb R^3\times\mathbb R$ be open. A **scalar-vector potential pair** of class $C^k$ on $\Omega$, for an integer $k\ge1$, is a pair $(\varphi,A)$ with $\varphi:\Omega\to\mathbb R$ and $A:\Omega\to\mathbb R^3$ each of class $C^k$ in the sense of [[def-ck-euclidean-maps-and-diffeomorphisms]], the components of $A$ being of class $C^k$ separately; the pair is **smooth** when both members are $C^\infty$, and **continuous**, or of class $C^0$, when both members are continuous. A pair defined on a set of the form $\mathbb R^3\times[t_0,T]$ with $t_0<T$ is of class $C^k$, $k\ge1$, **in the extension sense** when there are an open interval $J\supset[t_0,T]$ and a potential pair of class $C^k$ on the open set $\mathbb R^3\times J$ whose restriction to $\mathbb R^3\times[t_0,T]$ the given pair is; the same wording is used for $C^\infty$ and for the single functions $\varphi$ and $\chi$ below.

All operators $\nabla$, $\operatorname{div}$, $\operatorname{curl}$ and $\Delta$ below act on the three spatial coordinates with $t$ fixed: for $\Omega_t:=\{x\in\mathbb R^3:(x,t)\in\Omega\}$, apply the cited three-dimensional operators to the restrictions $x\mapsto\varphi(x,t)$, $x\mapsto A(x,t)$ or $x\mapsto u(x,t)$ on the open set $\Omega_t$. In particular $\nabla\varphi=(\partial_{x_1}\varphi,\partial_{x_2}\varphi,\partial_{x_3}\varphi)$ and $\Delta u=\sum_{i=1}^3\partial_{x_i}^2u$; $\partial_t$ differentiates only the time coordinate.

For a potential pair of class $C^k$ with $k\ge1$ its **electric field** and **magnetic field** are

$$E(\varphi,A):=-\nabla\varphi-\partial_tA,\qquad B(\varphi,A):=\operatorname{curl}A,$$

where $\nabla$ is the gradient of [[def-jacobian-matrix-and-gradient]], $\partial_t$ is the partial derivative of [[def-directional-and-partial-derivatives]], and $\operatorname{div}$ and $\operatorname{curl}$ are those of [[def-divergence-and-curl-of-a-c1-vector-field]]. Both $E(\varphi,A)$ and $B(\varphi,A)$ are maps $\Omega\to\mathbb R^3$ of class $C^{k-1}$.

For $k\ge1$ the **Lorenz divergence** of the pair is the function

$$G(\varphi,A):=\operatorname{div}A+c^{-2}\partial_t\varphi,$$

also of class $C^{k-1}$, and the pair is **in Lorenz gauge** on $\Omega$ when $G(\varphi,A)=0$ throughout $\Omega$.

For $k\ge2$ and a function $\chi:\Omega\to\mathbb R$ of class $C^k$, a **gauge function**, the **gauge transform** of the pair is

$$T_{\chi}(\varphi,A):=(\varphi-\partial_t\chi,\ A+\nabla\chi),$$

again a potential pair, of class $C^{k-1}$.

Finally, for a function $u:\Omega\to\mathbb R$ of class $C^2$ put

$$Wu:=c^{-2}\partial_t^2u-\Delta u,$$

with $\Delta$ the Laplacian of [[def-laplacian-of-a-c2-function]] and $\partial_t^2$ the second partial derivative in $t$ ([[def-directional-and-partial-derivatives]]); this is the normalization $W=c^{-2}\Box_c$ of the wave operator $\Box_c=\partial_t^2-c^2\Delta$ of speed $c$ of [[def-wave-equation-cauchy-data-and-wave-speed]]. For a map $U:\Omega\to\mathbb R^m$ of class $C^2$ with components $U_1,\dots,U_m$, one writes $WU:=(WU_1,\dots,WU_m)$ componentwise.

Nothing in this definition asserts that a gauge function with prescribed auxiliary data exists, that every potential pair is gauge equivalent to a pair in Lorenz gauge, or that $Wu=g$ is solvable: those are conclusions with their own hypotheses. The signs $-\nabla\varphi-\partial_tA$ and $A+\nabla\chi$, the factor $c^{-2}$ in $G$, and the spelling *Lorenz* are part of the convention.

Let $c>0$, let $U\cong I\times\Omega$ be the laboratory region of [[def-em-lab-geometry]] with its restricted inertial chart, let fields and units be those of [[def-em-fields]] and [[def-em-si-conventions]], and let the scalar-vector potential vocabulary on that region be that of [[def-em-potential-gauge-and-field-conventions]]: a **potential pair** $(\varphi,A)$ of class $C^k$ on $\Omega\times I$ consists of $\varphi:\Omega\times I\to\mathbb R$ and $A:\Omega\times I\to\mathbb R^3$ of class $C^k$ jointly in the sense of [[def-ck-euclidean-maps-and-diffeomorphisms]], and for a non-open time interval $I$ the joint classes in this item are read in the open-neighbourhood restriction convention of [[lem-em-joint-smooth-potentials]] (for open $I$ this is the ordinary class of [[def-ck-euclidean-maps-and-diffeomorphisms]]); for $k\ge1$ the **field pair** is

$$E(\varphi,A):=-\nabla\varphi-\partial_tA,\qquad B(\varphi,A):=\operatorname{curl}A,$$

where $\nabla$ is the gradient, $\operatorname{div}$ and $\operatorname{curl}$ are those of [[def-divergence-and-curl-of-a-c1-vector-field]], and $\partial_t$ is the partial derivative at fixed position of [[def-directional-and-partial-derivatives]]. For $k\ge1$ the **Lorenz divergence** of the pair is $G(\varphi,A):=\operatorname{div}A+c^{-2}\partial_t\varphi$. The definitions in this item are stated on the laboratory region; the framework's fields are those of [[def-em-fields]], and no field equation is assumed anywhere below.

(a) [Representations] Let $k\ge2$ be an integer and let $(E,B)$ be a field pair of class $C^{k-1}$ on $\Omega\times I$, meaning $E,B:\Omega\times I\to\mathbb R^3$ of class $C^{k-1}$ jointly as in [[def-em-fields]]. A **potential representation of class $C^k$** of $(E,B)$ is a potential pair $(\varphi,A)$ of class $C^k$ on $\Omega\times I$ whose field pair is $(E,B)$, that is, $E=-\nabla\varphi-\partial_tA$ and $B=\operatorname{curl}A$ on $\Omega\times I$. More generally, a potential pair of class $C^1$ represents a specified field pair whenever these two identities hold, even if the fields have greater regularity than the defining derivatives alone guarantee. This definition asserts neither existence nor uniqueness. On a star-shaped spatial region [[pthm-em-spacetime-potentials]] supplies $\varphi\in C^{r-1}$ and $A\in C^r$ for jointly $C^r$ field data, $r\ge2$, and smooth potentials for smooth data; it does not assert a $C^r$ scalar potential for merely $C^r$ data. Equality of field pairs does not by itself assert gauge relatedness on an arbitrary region; a converse needs its own domain and regularity hypotheses.

(b) [Gauge functions and gauge equivalence] A **gauge function** of class $C^m$, $m\ge2$, on $\Omega\times I$ is a function $\chi:\Omega\times I\to\mathbb R$ of class $C^m$ jointly; its **gauge transformation** sends a potential pair $(\varphi,A)$ of class $C^m$ to

$$T_\chi(\varphi,A):=(\varphi-\partial_t\chi,\ A+\nabla\chi),$$

a potential pair of class $C^{m-1}$. Two potential pairs are **gauge related** when one is the gauge transform of the other by some gauge function. On pairs and generators of class $C^\infty$, $T_0$ is the identity and $T_{\chi_1}\bigl(T_{\chi_2}(\varphi,A)\bigr)=T_{\chi_1+\chi_2}(\varphi,A)$ for all $C^\infty$ generators $\chi_1,\chi_2$; hence gauge relatedness is an equivalence relation on the $C^\infty$ potential pairs, the inverse of $T_\chi$ being $T_{-\chi}$. For a fixed finite class the transform drops one order, and relatedness is used only through the transform it records.

(c) [Conditions] A potential pair is **in Lorenz gauge** on $\Omega\times I$ when $G(\varphi,A)=\operatorname{div}A+c^{-2}\partial_t\varphi=0$ throughout $\Omega\times I$, and **in Coulomb gauge** in the chosen spatial chart when $\operatorname{div}A=0$ throughout $\Omega\times I$. These are properties of a pair in the stated conventions. The existence of a gauge function achieving either condition, with or without prescribed initial or boundary data, is a separate PDE conclusion with its own hypotheses and is not asserted by this definition.

(d) [Physical status] The physical content of a representation is its field pair $(E,B)$ of [[def-em-fields]]; the values of $\varphi$, of $A$ and of any gauge function are convention dependent and are auxiliary, and gauge related representations have the same field pair. The scalar potential $\varphi$ carries the volt, the vector potential $A$ carries the tesla metre, and a gauge function carries V s $=$ T m$^2$, so its time derivative and gradient have the units of $\varphi$ and $A$, respectively, consistently with [[def-em-si-conventions]]. No value of $\varphi$ or $A$ is by itself an observable or evidence for a field.

Let $c>0$, let $\Omega\subseteq\mathbb R^3$ be open, let $I\subseteq\mathbb R$ be an interval with at least two elements ([[def-interval]]), let $k\ge2$ be an integer, let $(\varphi,A)$ be a potential pair of class $C^k$ jointly on $\Omega\times I$ and let $\chi$ be a gauge function of class $C^k$ jointly on $\Omega\times I$, all in the conventions of [[def-em-potential-gauge-and-field-conventions]] and [[def-em-gauge-transformation]]: $E(\varphi,A)=-\nabla\varphi-\partial_tA$, $B(\varphi,A)=\operatorname{curl}A$ and $T_\chi(\varphi,A)=(\varphi-\partial_t\chi,\ A+\nabla\chi)$; for a non-open $I$ the joint $C^k$ classes are read in the open-neighbourhood restriction convention of [[lem-em-joint-smooth-potentials]] (for open $I$ this is the ordinary class of [[def-ck-euclidean-maps-and-diffeomorphisms]]).

Then $T_\chi(\varphi,A)$ is a potential pair of class $C^{k-1}$ jointly on $\Omega\times I$ and its field pair is the field pair of $(\varphi,A)$:

$$E(T_\chi(\varphi,A))=E(\varphi,A),\qquad B(T_\chi(\varphi,A))=B(\varphi,A)\qquad\text{on }\Omega\times I,$$

the common values being maps $\Omega\times I\to\mathbb R^3$ of class $C^{k-1}$ jointly, that is, fields of the framework in the sense of [[def-em-fields]]. In particular gauge related potential representations of one field pair have equal field pairs: the electric and magnetic fields are gauge invariants of the framework, and no value of $\varphi$, of $A$ or of $\chi$ is asserted to be observable.

The proof uses only the defining formulas, the vanishing of $\operatorname{curl}\nabla\chi$ for the $C^2$ function $\chi$ and the equality of the time-space mixed partials $\partial_t\partial_i\chi=\partial_i\partial_t\chi$; no Maxwell equation, no hypothesis on $\Omega$ beyond openness, and no choice principle is used.

Let $U\subseteq\mathbb R^3$ be open and let $\phi:U\to\mathbb R$ be $C^2$. Then $\nabla\phi$ is a $C^1$ field on $U$ and

$$\operatorname{curl}\nabla\phi=0\qquad\text{on }U.$$

If $f,g:U\to\mathbb R^n$ are totally differentiable at $a$ and $c\in\mathbb R$, then $f+g$ and $cf$ are totally differentiable at $a$, with

$$D(f+g)(a)=Df(a)+Dg(a),\qquad D(cf)(a)=cDf(a).$$

Let $U\subseteq\mathbb R^m$, $a\in U$, $v\in\mathbb R^m$, and $f:U\to\mathbb R^n$. If the line map $t\mapsto f(a+tv)$ is defined near $0$, its derivative at $0$ is the **directional derivative**

$$D_vf(a):=\lim_{t\to0}\frac{f(a+tv)-f(a)}{t}.$$

For a standard basis vector $e_j$ ([[lem-standard-basis-of-f-n]]), $D_{e_j}f(a)$ is the **$j$th partial derivative**, written $\partial_jf(a)$. These are ordinary vector-valued one-variable derivatives in the sense of [[def-vector-valued-derivative-and-integral]].

Let $n\ge1$, let $U\subseteq\mathbb R^n$ be open and let $F=(F_0,\ldots,F_{n-1}):U\to\mathbb R^n$ be $C^1$ in the componentwise Euclidean sense of [[def-ck-euclidean-maps-and-diffeomorphisms]]. Then the **divergence** of $F$ is $\operatorname{div}F:=\sum_{i<n}\partial_iF_i$, the function $U\to\mathbb R$ whose value at $p$ is $\sum_{i<n}\partial_iF_i(p)$. The partial derivatives are those of [[def-directional-and-partial-derivatives]], and the sum is the finite sum used throughout [[def-euclidean-inner-product]]. Since each $\partial_iF_i$ is continuous on $U$, so is $\operatorname{div}F$.

Now let $n=3$ and let $F:U\to\mathbb R^3$ be $C^1$ on an open $U\subseteq\mathbb R^3$. Following [[def-cross-product-in-r3]], write the three coordinates of a point and of a vector as $x,y,z$ rather than $0,1,2$, so that $F=(F_x,F_y,F_z)$ means $F=(F_0,F_1,F_2)$ and $\partial_x,\partial_y,\partial_z$ are $\partial_0,\partial_1,\partial_2$. With that naming, the **curl** of $F$ is $\operatorname{curl}F:=(\partial_yF_z-\partial_zF_y,\ \partial_zF_x-\partial_xF_z,\ \partial_xF_y-\partial_yF_x)$, a map $U\to\mathbb R^3$ each of whose coordinates is continuous on $U$. In this naming the divergence reads $\operatorname{div}F=\partial_xF_x+\partial_yF_y+\partial_zF_z$.

Both operators are defined pointwise from the first partial derivatives of the components, so no differentiability of $F$ beyond $C^1$ is used and no orientation or metric structure enters beyond the standard coordinates of [[def-jacobian-matrix-and-gradient]]. For a $C^1$ scalar function $f$ on $U$, the gradient $\nabla f=(\partial_0f,\ldots,\partial_{n-1}f)$ is that of [[def-jacobian-matrix-and-gradient]]; in the three-coordinate naming, $\nabla f=(\partial_xf,\partial_yf,\partial_zf)$.

Let the laboratory region $U\cong I\times\Omega$, its spatial Euclidean structure
and its units be those of [[def-em-lab-geometry]] and
[[def-em-si-conventions]], and let $k\ge1$. An **electric field of class
$C^k$** on the region is a map $E:\Omega\times I\to\mathbb R^3$ that is of class
$C^k$ in the sense of [[def-ck-euclidean-maps-and-diffeomorphisms]]; a
**magnetic field of class $C^k$** is a map $B:\Omega\times I\to\mathbb R^3$ of
the same class. At fixed $t\in I$ the maps $E(\cdot,t),B(\cdot,t):\Omega\to
\mathbb R^3$ are real spatial vector fields on the region $\Omega$, read in the
$\delta$-orthonormal basis $(e_1,e_2,e_3)$ of the frame. The framework uses:
$C^1$ fields in the classical Maxwell branch, $C^2$ fields where second or
mixed time-space derivatives of the fields appear, and $C^\infty$ fields in
the smooth existence branches; every statement carries its own regularity and
no regularity beyond it is asserted.

Conventions:

(a) The **polar-vector** and **axial-vector** conventions mean the following
component rules under a spatial orthogonal coordinate change $y'=Qy$, where
$Q$ is a real $3\times3$ matrix with $Q^{\mathsf T}Q=I_3$. Transpose,
matrix product and identity are those of [[def-transpose-of-a-matrix]] and
[[def-matrix-product-and-identity-matrix]], and $\det Q$ is the determinant
of [[def-determinant-of-a-square-matrix]]. At corresponding
points $E'(y',t)=QE(y,t)$ and $B'(y',t)=(\det Q)QB(y,t)$. Thus polar and axial
components agree in their transformation rule when $\det Q=1$ and differ by
a sign when $\det Q=-1$. These rules specify the orientation convention;
the adopted inertial descriptions have positive orientation, and no physical
orientation-reversing change of description is adopted here.

(b) The fields are defined by their values on $\Omega\times I$, and no value at
a point of singular source support is asserted.

(c) $E$ carries V m$^{-1}$ and $B$ carries T.

(d) The identification of the pair $(E,B)$ with the components of an
alternating two-form, including its transformation behaviour, is made in the
framework's electromagnetic two-form definition on this page and is not
presupposed here.

**Regularity convention for a possibly non-open parameter interval.** Let $U\subseteq\mathbb R^3$ be open, let $I\subseteq\mathbb R$ be an interval and let $k\in\mathbb N$. A map on $U\times I$ is **jointly $C^k$** when it is the restriction of a $C^k$ map on some open neighbourhood $N\subseteq\mathbb R^4$ of $U\times I$, in the sense of [[def-ck-euclidean-maps-and-diffeomorphisms]]; it is **jointly $C^\infty$** when it is the restriction of one smooth map on such an open neighbourhood. For open $I$ these are exactly the usual open-domain classes; at included endpoints of a nondegenerate interval, time derivatives are the corresponding relative one-sided derivatives. For empty or singleton $I$ the convention still asserts extension existence and the spatial identities below, but it does not determine time jets uniquely from the restricted values alone. The convention does not require a fixed uniform enlargement of an unbounded $I$.

**Vector witness.** Let $U\subseteq\mathbb R^3$ be open and star-shaped with centre $a\in U$ ([[def-star-shaped-open-subset-of-rn]]), let $I\subseteq\mathbb R$ be an interval, let $k\ge1$, and let $B:U\times I\to\mathbb R^3$ be jointly $C^k$ with $\operatorname{div}B(\cdot,t)=0$ on $U$ for every $t\in I$ ([[def-divergence-and-curl-of-a-c1-vector-field]]). Then

$$A(x,t):=\int_0^1s\,B\bigl(a+s(x-a),t\bigr)\times(x-a)\,ds$$

is jointly $C^k$ on $U\times I$ and

$$\operatorname{curl}A(\cdot,t)=B(\cdot,t)\qquad(t\in I),$$

the curl being taken in the spatial variables and the cross product being that of [[def-cross-product-in-r3]].

**Scalar witness.** If in addition $C:U\times I\to\mathbb R^3$ is jointly $C^k$ with $\operatorname{curl}C(\cdot,t)=0$ on $U$ for every $t\in I$, then

$$\phi(x,t):=-\int_0^1\bigl\langle C\bigl(a+s(x-a),t\bigr),\,x-a\bigr\rangle\,ds$$

is jointly $C^k$ on $U\times I$ and

$$\nabla\phi(\cdot,t)=-C(\cdot,t)\qquad(t\in I),$$

the gradient and inner product being those of [[def-directional-and-partial-derivatives]] and [[def-euclidean-inner-product]]. For jointly $C^\infty$ data both potentials are jointly $C^\infty$. No global potential on a non-star-shaped open set is claimed, and the restrictions are continuous at included endpoints by joint regularity.

derivations.claim:
The general pure-gauge pair. The zero pair $(0,0)$ is a potential pair of class $C^2$ by [F1], and $\chi$ is a gauge function of class $C^2$, so the transform $T_\chi(0,0)=(-\partial_t\chi,\ 
abla\chi)$ is a potential pair of class $C^1$ by [F1]; its field pair is defined and, for a nondegenerate $I$, by [F2] with $k=2$ equals the field pair of $(0,0)$. For singleton $I$, apply [F2] on open spatial-time boxes in the chosen extension neighbourhood and then restrict the ambient pair and its jets to $\Omega	imes I$; these local computations cover the singleton slice. For an empty product the identities are vacuous. That field pair is $E(0,0)=-
abla0-\partial_t0=0$ and $B(0,0)=\operatorname{curl}0=0$ by [F1] and [F4], because all first derivatives of the constant zero pair vanish. Hence $E(\varphi,A)=0$; separately, $B(\varphi,A)=\operatorname{curl}
abla\chi=0$ by [F3] applied to the $C^2$ function $\chi$. Thus every $C^2$ generator produces a pure-gauge pair, and the resulting field pair is the zero field pair of [F5].

The constant instance. For $\chi(x,t)=a\cdot x-\beta t$ on $\mathbb R^3\times\mathbb R$, [F4] gives $\nabla\chi=a$ and $\partial_t\chi=-\beta$, so $(\varphi,A)=T_\chi(0,0)=(\beta,a)$ as constant maps on $\mathbb R^3\times\mathbb R$. For this constant pair, $E=-\nabla\beta-\partial_t a=0$ and $B=\operatorname{curl}a=0$ by [F1] and [F4]: the gradient of the constant scalar $\beta$ and the time derivative of the constant field $a$ vanish, and the curl of the constant field $a$ vanishes because each of its first partial derivatives is zero.

The zero-parameter branch and the nonzero witness. The constant pair $(\beta,a)$ equals the zero pair $(0,0)$ if and only if $\beta=0$ and $a=0$, equality of maps on the nonempty set $\mathbb R^3\times\mathbb R$ being componentwise equality of the constants; at $\beta=0$, $a=0$ the generator is $\chi=0$ and $T_0$ is the identity by [F1], so the zero pair is recovered. Taking instead $\beta=0$ and $a=e_1$ gives a pair $(\varphi,A)=(0,e_1)$ that is not the zero pair, while by steps 1.1 and 2.1 its field pair is $(0,0)$: explicitly $\varphi=0$, $A=(1,0,0)$ are constant, so $E=-\nabla0-\partial_t e_1=0$ and $B=\operatorname{curl}e_1=0$ by [F4]. Two distinct potential pairs therefore have the same field pair, and the map from potential pairs to field pairs of [F5] is not injective.

Conclusion and scope. Every $C^2$ gauge generator gives a potential pair with the zero field pair (step 1.1); the linear family $\chi(x,t)=a\cdot x-\beta t$ realizes the constant pairs $(\beta,a)$, with the zero pair exactly at the zero parameters and the witness $(0,e_1)$ distinct from $(0,0)$ while still representing the zero field pair (steps 2.1 and 3.1). No Maxwell equation, source configuration, choice principle or empirical situation is used, and no nonzero value of $\varphi$ or $A$ is asserted to be evidence for a nonzero field.

Let $c>0$ and let $\Omega\subseteq\mathbb R^3\times\mathbb R$ be open. A **scalar-vector potential pair** of class $C^k$ on $\Omega$, for an integer $k\ge1$, is a pair $(\varphi,A)$ with $\varphi:\Omega\to\mathbb R$ and $A:\Omega\to\mathbb R^3$ each of class $C^k$ in the sense of [[def-ck-euclidean-maps-and-diffeomorphisms]], the components of $A$ being of class $C^k$ separately; the pair is **smooth** when both members are $C^\infty$, and **continuous**, or of class $C^0$, when both members are continuous. A pair defined on a set of the form $\mathbb R^3\times[t_0,T]$ with $t_0<T$ is of class $C^k$, $k\ge1$, **in the extension sense** when there are an open interval $J\supset[t_0,T]$ and a potential pair of class $C^k$ on the open set $\mathbb R^3\times J$ whose restriction to $\mathbb R^3\times[t_0,T]$ the given pair is; the same wording is used for $C^\infty$ and for the single functions $\varphi$ and $\chi$ below.

All operators $\nabla$, $\operatorname{div}$, $\operatorname{curl}$ and $\Delta$ below act on the three spatial coordinates with $t$ fixed: for $\Omega_t:=\{x\in\mathbb R^3:(x,t)\in\Omega\}$, apply the cited three-dimensional operators to the restrictions $x\mapsto\varphi(x,t)$, $x\mapsto A(x,t)$ or $x\mapsto u(x,t)$ on the open set $\Omega_t$. In particular $\nabla\varphi=(\partial_{x_1}\varphi,\partial_{x_2}\varphi,\partial_{x_3}\varphi)$ and $\Delta u=\sum_{i=1}^3\partial_{x_i}^2u$; $\partial_t$ differentiates only the time coordinate.

For a potential pair of class $C^k$ with $k\ge1$ its **electric field** and **magnetic field** are

$$E(\varphi,A):=-\nabla\varphi-\partial_tA,\qquad B(\varphi,A):=\operatorname{curl}A,$$

where $\nabla$ is the gradient of [[def-jacobian-matrix-and-gradient]], $\partial_t$ is the partial derivative of [[def-directional-and-partial-derivatives]], and $\operatorname{div}$ and $\operatorname{curl}$ are those of [[def-divergence-and-curl-of-a-c1-vector-field]]. Both $E(\varphi,A)$ and $B(\varphi,A)$ are maps $\Omega\to\mathbb R^3$ of class $C^{k-1}$.

For $k\ge1$ the **Lorenz divergence** of the pair is the function

$$G(\varphi,A):=\operatorname{div}A+c^{-2}\partial_t\varphi,$$

also of class $C^{k-1}$, and the pair is **in Lorenz gauge** on $\Omega$ when $G(\varphi,A)=0$ throughout $\Omega$.

For $k\ge2$ and a function $\chi:\Omega\to\mathbb R$ of class $C^k$, a **gauge function**, the **gauge transform** of the pair is

$$T_{\chi}(\varphi,A):=(\varphi-\partial_t\chi,\ A+\nabla\chi),$$

again a potential pair, of class $C^{k-1}$.

Finally, for a function $u:\Omega\to\mathbb R$ of class $C^2$ put

$$Wu:=c^{-2}\partial_t^2u-\Delta u,$$

with $\Delta$ the Laplacian of [[def-laplacian-of-a-c2-function]] and $\partial_t^2$ the second partial derivative in $t$ ([[def-directional-and-partial-derivatives]]); this is the normalization $W=c^{-2}\Box_c$ of the wave operator $\Box_c=\partial_t^2-c^2\Delta$ of speed $c$ of [[def-wave-equation-cauchy-data-and-wave-speed]]. For a map $U:\Omega\to\mathbb R^m$ of class $C^2$ with components $U_1,\dots,U_m$, one writes $WU:=(WU_1,\dots,WU_m)$ componentwise.

Nothing in this definition asserts that a gauge function with prescribed auxiliary data exists, that every potential pair is gauge equivalent to a pair in Lorenz gauge, or that $Wu=g$ is solvable: those are conclusions with their own hypotheses. The signs $-\nabla\varphi-\partial_tA$ and $A+\nabla\chi$, the factor $c^{-2}$ in $G$, and the spelling *Lorenz* are part of the convention.

Let $c>0$, let $U\cong I\times\Omega$ be the laboratory region of [[def-em-lab-geometry]] with its restricted inertial chart, let fields and units be those of [[def-em-fields]] and [[def-em-si-conventions]], and let the scalar-vector potential vocabulary on that region be that of [[def-em-potential-gauge-and-field-conventions]]: a **potential pair** $(\varphi,A)$ of class $C^k$ on $\Omega\times I$ consists of $\varphi:\Omega\times I\to\mathbb R$ and $A:\Omega\times I\to\mathbb R^3$ of class $C^k$ jointly in the sense of [[def-ck-euclidean-maps-and-diffeomorphisms]], and for a non-open time interval $I$ the joint classes in this item are read in the open-neighbourhood restriction convention of [[lem-em-joint-smooth-potentials]] (for open $I$ this is the ordinary class of [[def-ck-euclidean-maps-and-diffeomorphisms]]); for $k\ge1$ the **field pair** is

$$E(\varphi,A):=-\nabla\varphi-\partial_tA,\qquad B(\varphi,A):=\operatorname{curl}A,$$

where $\nabla$ is the gradient, $\operatorname{div}$ and $\operatorname{curl}$ are those of [[def-divergence-and-curl-of-a-c1-vector-field]], and $\partial_t$ is the partial derivative at fixed position of [[def-directional-and-partial-derivatives]]. For $k\ge1$ the **Lorenz divergence** of the pair is $G(\varphi,A):=\operatorname{div}A+c^{-2}\partial_t\varphi$. The definitions in this item are stated on the laboratory region; the framework's fields are those of [[def-em-fields]], and no field equation is assumed anywhere below.

(a) [Representations] Let $k\ge2$ be an integer and let $(E,B)$ be a field pair of class $C^{k-1}$ on $\Omega\times I$, meaning $E,B:\Omega\times I\to\mathbb R^3$ of class $C^{k-1}$ jointly as in [[def-em-fields]]. A **potential representation of class $C^k$** of $(E,B)$ is a potential pair $(\varphi,A)$ of class $C^k$ on $\Omega\times I$ whose field pair is $(E,B)$, that is, $E=-\nabla\varphi-\partial_tA$ and $B=\operatorname{curl}A$ on $\Omega\times I$. More generally, a potential pair of class $C^1$ represents a specified field pair whenever these two identities hold, even if the fields have greater regularity than the defining derivatives alone guarantee. This definition asserts neither existence nor uniqueness. On a star-shaped spatial region [[pthm-em-spacetime-potentials]] supplies $\varphi\in C^{r-1}$ and $A\in C^r$ for jointly $C^r$ field data, $r\ge2$, and smooth potentials for smooth data; it does not assert a $C^r$ scalar potential for merely $C^r$ data. Equality of field pairs does not by itself assert gauge relatedness on an arbitrary region; a converse needs its own domain and regularity hypotheses.

(b) [Gauge functions and gauge equivalence] A **gauge function** of class $C^m$, $m\ge2$, on $\Omega\times I$ is a function $\chi:\Omega\times I\to\mathbb R$ of class $C^m$ jointly; its **gauge transformation** sends a potential pair $(\varphi,A)$ of class $C^m$ to

$$T_\chi(\varphi,A):=(\varphi-\partial_t\chi,\ A+\nabla\chi),$$

a potential pair of class $C^{m-1}$. Two potential pairs are **gauge related** when one is the gauge transform of the other by some gauge function. On pairs and generators of class $C^\infty$, $T_0$ is the identity and $T_{\chi_1}\bigl(T_{\chi_2}(\varphi,A)\bigr)=T_{\chi_1+\chi_2}(\varphi,A)$ for all $C^\infty$ generators $\chi_1,\chi_2$; hence gauge relatedness is an equivalence relation on the $C^\infty$ potential pairs, the inverse of $T_\chi$ being $T_{-\chi}$. For a fixed finite class the transform drops one order, and relatedness is used only through the transform it records.

(c) [Conditions] A potential pair is **in Lorenz gauge** on $\Omega\times I$ when $G(\varphi,A)=\operatorname{div}A+c^{-2}\partial_t\varphi=0$ throughout $\Omega\times I$, and **in Coulomb gauge** in the chosen spatial chart when $\operatorname{div}A=0$ throughout $\Omega\times I$. These are properties of a pair in the stated conventions. The existence of a gauge function achieving either condition, with or without prescribed initial or boundary data, is a separate PDE conclusion with its own hypotheses and is not asserted by this definition.

(d) [Physical status] The physical content of a representation is its field pair $(E,B)$ of [[def-em-fields]]; the values of $\varphi$, of $A$ and of any gauge function are convention dependent and are auxiliary, and gauge related representations have the same field pair. The scalar potential $\varphi$ carries the volt, the vector potential $A$ carries the tesla metre, and a gauge function carries V s $=$ T m$^2$, so its time derivative and gradient have the units of $\varphi$ and $A$, respectively, consistently with [[def-em-si-conventions]]. No value of $\varphi$ or $A$ is by itself an observable or evidence for a field.

Let $n\ge1$, let $U\subseteq\mathbb R^n$ be open and let $f:U\to\mathbb R$ be $C^2$ in the sense of [[def-ck-and-multi-index-notation-in-several-variables]]. Then $\nabla f$ is a $C^1$ field on $U$ by [[def-ck-euclidean-maps-and-diffeomorphisms]], since each of its components $\partial_if$ has continuous first partial derivatives, so its divergence is defined; the **Laplacian** of $f$ is

$$\Delta f:=\operatorname{div}\nabla f=\sum_{i<n}\partial_i\partial_if,$$

with the gradient of [[def-jacobian-matrix-and-gradient]] and the divergence of [[def-divergence-and-curl-of-a-c1-vector-field]]. A $C^2$ function with $\Delta f=0$ on $U$ is called **harmonic** on $U$.

For a $C^2$ map $F=(F_0,\ldots,F_{q-1}):U\to\mathbb R^q$, whose components are $C^2$ by [[def-ck-euclidean-maps-and-diffeomorphisms]], $\Delta F$ is the field whose $i$th coordinate is $\Delta F_i$. In the three-coordinate naming of this page, $\Delta f=\partial_x\partial_xf+\partial_y\partial_yf+\partial_z\partial_zf$ and $\Delta F=(\Delta F_x,\Delta F_y,\Delta F_z)$.

Let the laboratory region $U\cong I\times\Omega$, its spatial Euclidean structure
and its units be those of [[def-em-lab-geometry]] and
[[def-em-si-conventions]], and let $k\ge1$. An **electric field of class
$C^k$** on the region is a map $E:\Omega\times I\to\mathbb R^3$ that is of class
$C^k$ in the sense of [[def-ck-euclidean-maps-and-diffeomorphisms]]; a
**magnetic field of class $C^k$** is a map $B:\Omega\times I\to\mathbb R^3$ of
the same class. At fixed $t\in I$ the maps $E(\cdot,t),B(\cdot,t):\Omega\to
\mathbb R^3$ are real spatial vector fields on the region $\Omega$, read in the
$\delta$-orthonormal basis $(e_1,e_2,e_3)$ of the frame. The framework uses:
$C^1$ fields in the classical Maxwell branch, $C^2$ fields where second or
mixed time-space derivatives of the fields appear, and $C^\infty$ fields in
the smooth existence branches; every statement carries its own regularity and
no regularity beyond it is asserted.

Conventions:

(a) The **polar-vector** and **axial-vector** conventions mean the following
component rules under a spatial orthogonal coordinate change $y'=Qy$, where
$Q$ is a real $3\times3$ matrix with $Q^{\mathsf T}Q=I_3$. Transpose,
matrix product and identity are those of [[def-transpose-of-a-matrix]] and
[[def-matrix-product-and-identity-matrix]], and $\det Q$ is the determinant
of [[def-determinant-of-a-square-matrix]]. At corresponding
points $E'(y',t)=QE(y,t)$ and $B'(y',t)=(\det Q)QB(y,t)$. Thus polar and axial
components agree in their transformation rule when $\det Q=1$ and differ by
a sign when $\det Q=-1$. These rules specify the orientation convention;
the adopted inertial descriptions have positive orientation, and no physical
orientation-reversing change of description is adopted here.

(b) The fields are defined by their values on $\Omega\times I$, and no value at
a point of singular source support is asserted.

(c) $E$ carries V m$^{-1}$ and $B$ carries T.

(d) The identification of the pair $(E,B)$ with the components of an
alternating two-form, including its transformation behaviour, is made in the
framework's electromagnetic two-form definition on this page and is not
presupposed here.

Let $c>0$, let $\Omega\subseteq\mathbb R^3$ be open, let $I\subseteq\mathbb R$ be an interval with at least two elements ([[def-interval]]), let $k\ge2$ be an integer, let $(\varphi,A)$ be a potential pair of class $C^k$ jointly on $\Omega\times I$ and let $\chi$ be a gauge function of class $C^k$ jointly on $\Omega\times I$, all in the conventions of [[def-em-potential-gauge-and-field-conventions]] and [[def-em-gauge-transformation]]: $E(\varphi,A)=-\nabla\varphi-\partial_tA$, $B(\varphi,A)=\operatorname{curl}A$ and $T_\chi(\varphi,A)=(\varphi-\partial_t\chi,\ A+\nabla\chi)$; for a non-open $I$ the joint $C^k$ classes are read in the open-neighbourhood restriction convention of [[lem-em-joint-smooth-potentials]] (for open $I$ this is the ordinary class of [[def-ck-euclidean-maps-and-diffeomorphisms]]).

Then $T_\chi(\varphi,A)$ is a potential pair of class $C^{k-1}$ jointly on $\Omega\times I$ and its field pair is the field pair of $(\varphi,A)$:

$$E(T_\chi(\varphi,A))=E(\varphi,A),\qquad B(T_\chi(\varphi,A))=B(\varphi,A)\qquad\text{on }\Omega\times I,$$

the common values being maps $\Omega\times I\to\mathbb R^3$ of class $C^{k-1}$ jointly, that is, fields of the framework in the sense of [[def-em-fields]]. In particular gauge related potential representations of one field pair have equal field pairs: the electric and magnetic fields are gauge invariants of the framework, and no value of $\varphi$, of $A$ or of $\chi$ is asserted to be observable.

The proof uses only the defining formulas, the vanishing of $\operatorname{curl}\nabla\chi$ for the $C^2$ function $\chi$ and the equality of the time-space mixed partials $\partial_t\partial_i\chi=\partial_i\partial_t\chi$; no Maxwell equation, no hypothesis on $\Omega$ beyond openness, and no choice principle is used.

Let $c>0$, let $\Omega\subseteq\mathbb R^3$ be open, let $I\subseteq\mathbb R$ be an interval with at least two elements ([[def-interval]]), and let $(\varphi,A)$ be a potential pair of class $C^2$ jointly on $\Omega\times I$ in the restriction convention of [[lem-em-joint-smooth-potentials]] ([[def-em-potential-gauge-and-field-conventions]]): for open $I$ this is the ordinary open-domain class of [[def-ck-euclidean-maps-and-diffeomorphisms]], and for non-open $I$ the pair is the restriction of a $C^2$ pair on an open neighbourhood of $\Omega\times I$, with relative derivatives at included endpoints and no time jet beyond the restricted values. Write $(E,B)$ for the field pair of $(\varphi,A)$ ([[def-em-fields]]) and

$$G:=\operatorname{div}A+c^{-2}\partial_t\varphi,\qquad W:=c^{-2}\partial_t^2-\Delta$$

for the Lorenz divergence and the wave expression of [[def-em-potential-gauge-and-field-conventions]], with $\Delta$ the Laplacian of [[def-laplacian-of-a-c2-function]]. Let $\rho:\Omega\times I\to\mathbb R$ and $J:\Omega\times I\to\mathbb R^3$ be continuous source fields of the framework ([[def-em-sources]]).

(a) [Exact identities] Independently of any field equation,

$$\operatorname{div}E=W\varphi-\partial_tG,\qquad \operatorname{curl}B-c^{-2}\partial_tE=WA+\nabla G\qquad\text{on }\Omega\times I.$$

Consequently the sourced Maxwell equations of [[post-em-vacuum-maxwell]] hold for $(E,B,\rho,J)$ if and only if

$$W\varphi-\partial_tG=\frac{\rho}{\varepsilon_0},\qquad WA+\nabla G=\mu_0J\qquad\text{on }\Omega\times I,$$

with $\varepsilon_0=(\mu_0c^2)^{-1}$ the constant of that postulate.

(b) [Gauge shift] If $\chi:\Omega\times I\to\mathbb R$ is a gauge function of class $C^2$ jointly on $\Omega\times I$ ([[def-em-gauge-transformation]]), then $G(T_\chi(\varphi,A))=G-W\chi$ on $\Omega\times I$ and the transformed pair has the same field pair $(E,B)$ ([[pthm-em-gauge-invariance]]); hence $T_\chi(\varphi,A)$ is in Lorenz gauge if and only if $W\chi=G$ on $\Omega\times I$.

(c) [Decoupling in Lorenz gauge] Suppose in addition that the given pair is in Lorenz gauge, $G=0$ on $\Omega\times I$. Then its field pair solves the sourced Maxwell system of [[post-em-vacuum-maxwell]] if and only if the pair satisfies the decoupled sourced wave equations

$$W\varphi=\rho/\varepsilon_0,\qquad WA=\mu_0J\qquad\text{on }\Omega\times I.$$

The two source-free equations $\operatorname{div}B=0$ and $\operatorname{curl}E=-\partial_tB$ hold automatically for every potential pair of class $C^2$. For an arbitrary given potential pair, the conjunction of Lorenz gauge with these two wave equations implies the sourced Maxwell system, but Maxwell's equations alone do not impose $G=0$ on that representative: their exact equivalent conditions remain the residual equations of (a), whose right-hand sides retain $\partial_tG$ and $\nabla G$.

(d) [Residual generators] If the $C^2$ gauge function of (b) satisfies $W\chi=0$ on $\Omega\times I$, then the transform of a pair in Lorenz gauge is again in Lorenz gauge and has the same field pair. When $\Omega$ is nonempty the Lorenz condition does not determine the pair: the generator $\chi(x,t)=x_1$, read in numerical SI components with gauge units as in [[def-em-gauge-transformation]], has $W\chi=0$ and changes $A$ by the nonzero constant vector $(1,0,0)$.

(e) [Scope] The identities and equivalences are properties of the given $C^2$ representation. No gauge function with $W\chi=G$, and no generator meeting prescribed initial or boundary values, is asserted to exist; that is a separate PDE conclusion with its own hypotheses, treated by the gauge-reachability theorem later on this page. No boundary, decay or initial condition on the pair is imposed, and no empirical claim or observability of $\varphi$ or $A$ is included. A pair of class $C^1$ defines $E$, $B$ and $G$ but need not possess the second derivatives appearing in $W\varphi$, $WA$, $\Delta$ or $\partial_tG$, so $C^2$ is the exact standing regularity here.

Assume the Axiom of Countable Choice ($\mathrm{AC}_\omega$), carried through [[thm-em-wave-cauchy-kirchhoff]] and its sphere integrations ([[def-countable-choice]]). Let $c>0$, $t_0<T$, and let $(\varphi,A)$ be a potential pair of class $C^\infty$ on the slab $Q:=\mathbb R^3\times[t_0,T]$ in the extension sense of [[def-em-potential-gauge-and-field-conventions]]: $\varphi$ and $A$ are restrictions of $C^\infty$ functions on $\mathbb R^3\times J$ for some open interval $J\supset[t_0,T]$ ([[def-ck-euclidean-maps-and-diffeomorphisms]]). Put $G:=G(\varphi,A)=\operatorname{div}A+c^{-2}\partial_t\varphi$ and $W=c^{-2}\partial_t^2-\Delta$. Then:

(a) there is a gauge function $\chi:\mathbb R^3\times[t_0,T]\to\mathbb R$ of class $C^\infty$ in the extension sense with $\chi(\cdot,t_0)=0$, $\partial_t\chi(\cdot,t_0)=0$ and $W\chi=G$ on $\mathbb R^3\times(t_0,T)$;

(b) the gauge-transformed pair $T_\chi(\varphi,A)=(\varphi-\partial_t\chi,\,A+\nabla\chi)$ is again of class $C^\infty$ in the extension sense and its fields are unchanged:

$$E(T_\chi(\varphi,A))=E(\varphi,A),\qquad B(T_\chi(\varphi,A))=B(\varphi,A)\qquad\text{on }Q;$$

(c) the transformed pair is in Lorenz gauge: $G(T_\chi(\varphi,A))=G-W\chi=0$ on $\mathbb R^3\times(t_0,T)$;

(d) if $\chi_1,\chi_2$ are of class $C^2$ on $Q$ in the extension sense and $W\chi_1=W\chi_2=G$ on $\mathbb R^3\times(t_0,T)$, then $W(\chi_1-\chi_2)=0$ on $\mathbb R^3\times(t_0,T)$.

Nothing is asserted about prescribed boundary values of $\chi$ on a bounded spatial domain, about spatial decay of $\chi$, or about Lorenz gauge fixing for a cavity problem with prescribed boundary data; the older global gauge promise on bounded domains is outside this result.

Assume AC and Countable Choice carried by the variational and Sobolev suppliers ([[def-axiom-of-choice]], [[def-countable-choice]]). Let $\Omega$ be a bounded smooth graph domain in $\mathbb R^3$ ([[def-bounded-c-k-domain-and-boundary-charts]]), $\varepsilon>0$ constant and $J$ an open interval. Let the bulk datum $f$ be jointly smooth up to $\overline\Omega\times J$ in the all-mixed-derivative sense of the parameter-preserving extension supplier, and let boundary families $g_D,\kappa$ be smooth in a fixed finite boundary atlas $\times\,J$. Then the Dirichlet problem $-\varepsilon\Delta u=f$, $u|_{\partial\Omega}=g_D$ has a unique solution on $\Omega\times J$; it has a single smooth ambient continuation near the closed spatial domain $\times\,J$. The Neumann problem $-\varepsilon\Delta u=f$, $\varepsilon\partial_\nu u=\kappa$ has such a solution precisely when

$$\int_{\Omega_j}f(\cdot,t)+\int_{\partial\Omega_j}\kappa(\cdot,t)=0\quad\text{for each component and every }t\in J.$$

It is unique modulo a separately chosen spatial constant on each component at each time. The normalization $\int_{\Omega_j}u(\cdot,t)=0$ gives a unique smooth family. Both solution operations are linear in their data; time differentiation commutes with them. Smoothness and estimates are local in compact time subintervals, with no uniform-in-$J$ requirement. The smooth ambient continuations are auxiliary and are not unique off the closed physical spatial region.
